lessons.title: The atlas — what genomic surveillance is, and the four questions it answers
lessons.subtitle: The whole landscape on day one, so every later lesson has something to point at
lessons.description: Sixty applications sorted by the four questions genomic surveillance can answer, the molecule-to-decision chain, and the three things a consensus genome can never tell you.
topics: What a consensus genome cannot tell you
lessons.practical: Take the last three genomic surveillance claims you read. Sort each into one of the four questions, name its classical comparator, and note whether the evidence offered belongs to the question actually being asked.

quiz.question: A report states that a lineage is more transmissible, supporting it only with the observation that it grew as a share of sequenced samples over eight weeks. Which failure is this?
options: A question-2 claim, because share-of-sequences is fundamentally a geographic quantity
A question-4 claim supported by question-3 evidence that is itself confounded by sampling
A question-1 claim that should have used contact tracing as its comparator instead
A valid inference, since growth in sequence share is the operational definition of transmissibility
quiz.explanation: Transmissibility is a property of the pathogen (Q4) and needs a phenotypic or carefully-controlled epidemiological link. Growth in sequence share is Q3 evidence, and it is confounded by every change in who got sequenced. Answering one question with another question's evidence is the field's most common error.

quiz.question: Which statement about the molecule-to-decision chain is correct?
options: Sampling and metadata sit inside the chain, between the machine stage and the data stage
Information is preserved at each step of the chain provided the sequencing depth is adequate throughout the genome
Depth of coverage above the minimum threshold preserves within-host diversity all the way through to the tree
Information is only ever lost moving rightward, so the skill is knowing what each step discarded
quiz.explanation: Every step is a lossy compression: consensus discards within-host diversity, alignment discards unsequenced regions, the tree discards everything but topology and branch lengths. Nothing downstream recovers it. Sampling and metadata sit outside the chain and determine all of it.

quiz.question: Genomics is described as better at ruling transmission links out than in. What underlies the asymmetry?
options: Contact tracing supplies the negative evidence, so the genomic contribution is purely confirmatory
Exclusion requires no molecular clock estimate at all, whereas confirming a link requires a fully calibrated one
A large distance would require an improbable mutation burst; a small distance fits many histories
Consensus calling resolves genuine differences reliably but reports spurious identity whenever coverage is uneven between samples
quiz.explanation: With well under one substitution per transmission, identical genomes are consistent with direct transmission, with a short unsampled chain, and with a common source. A large distance, by contrast, would require far more mutation than the clock allows — which is why it is strong evidence against a link.

quiz.question: Which of these can a consensus genome NOT tell you, however good the sequencing was?
options: How far this sample sits from another sample in the same alignment
Which lineage the sample belongs to under a current nomenclature scheme
Whether the sample carries a documented drug-resistance substitution
Whether a minority resistant subpopulation is present in the patient
quiz.explanation: Consensus calling reports the majority base at each position and discards everything below the threshold. Minority variants, mixed infection and transmission bottlenecks all require the reads. The other three are exactly what a consensus genome is for.

quiz.question: A surveillance programme reports 8,400 genomes produced last year. By this course's framing, what is the deficiency?
options: The count should be normalised against the number of reported cases so that programmes of different sizes can be compared
It omits the genome completeness distribution, which is what determines how many of those genomes were analysable at all
Genome count is not a measure of decisions changed, which is what a programme is for
Genome count without a stated sequencing platform is not a comparable figure
quiz.explanation: Volume is the metric most easily produced and least connected to purpose. The defensible account names decisions that came out differently. Completeness and platform matter, but they are inputs to the same question rather than the question itself.

exercises.label: Conceptual
exercises.prompt: Three claims, each from a real headline shape. Sort each into one of the four questions, name the classical comparator it must beat, and say what evidence it owes you.
questions: “Sequencing revealed the outbreak began two months earlier than anyone realised.”
“Genomic analysis confirmed the new variant spreads 40% faster.”
“Whole genome sequencing linked the hospital cluster to a single index patient.”
exercises.guidance: 1 is Q3 (dynamics) and owes you the sampling frame plus the interval, not a point estimate. 2 is written as Q4 but is almost always supported only by Q3 evidence — growth in sequence share — which is confounded by who got sequenced; it owes a phenotypic or carefully controlled epidemiological link. 3 is Q1 and owes the local background diversity; note also that ‘linked’ and ‘identified the index patient’ are different and much stronger claims.

exercises.label: Read the output
exercises.prompt: A national genomic surveillance dashboard reports the figures below for one month. Answer the three questions.
questions: What does the national row “Lineage A 55%” actually describe, stated precisely?
A colleague concludes that Lineage B is expanding because it dominates in Northern province. What is wrong with that inference, and what would you need to test it?
Compute sequences-per-case for each province. What is the ratio between the highest and the lowest, and what does that do to any national proportion estimate?
exercises.guidance: The national row describes the 329 sequenced samples, not the 1,759 cases — and the sequenced set is dominated by Central and Western, which together supplied 86% of sequences but 30% of cases. Northern’s 79% rests on 14 sequences (roughly ±11 percentage points at best, and that assumes random sampling within the province). Sequences per case: Central 0.46, Northern 0.04, Eastern 0.04, Western 0.81 — a twentyfold range. The ‘national’ proportions are a weighted average of provinces sampled at wildly different intensities, so they are closer to a description of Central and Western than of the country.

exercises.label: Three of six
exercises.prompt: Exactly three of these statements are correct.

statements.text: A consensus genome cannot tell you whether a minority drug-resistant subpopulation is present in the patient.
Clade size on a phylogeny is a direct measure of how much transmission that clade caused.
Genomic data excludes transmission links more reliably than it confirms them.
An ancestral-state reconstruction is a statement about the epidemic, independent of where sequencing happened.
A mutation identified in a surveillance dataset is a hypothesis about a phenotype, not a phenotype.
Because the chain from molecule to decision is lossy, sequencing more deeply at the final step recovers what earlier steps discarded.

exercises.guidance: 1, 3 and 5. Clade size tracks sampling at least as much as transmission; ancestral-state reconstruction places origins where sequencing is dense; and information lost at an earlier step of the chain is not recoverable at a later one — depth at the tree stage cannot restore within-host diversity that consensus calling already discarded.

exercises.label: Scaffolded
exercises.prompt: Below is a finished sentence from a report. Rewrite it so it states the observation and the inference separately, and hedges the inference in proportion to the sampling. The structure is given; supply the content.
exercises.guidance: Observation: genomes from Mongbwalu showed substantial diversity and emerged from relatively deep parts of the tree. Inference: this is consistent with Mongbwalu being an early or originating focus. Alternative: Mongbwalu was sampled early and heavily, and deep-and-diverse is exactly what dense early sampling also produces. The published version of this sentence uses ‘suggesting’ and ‘possible’, and those hedges are load-bearing rather than decorative.

lessons.title: Two clocks — why a pathogen genome carries epidemiological information at all
lessons.subtitle: One multiplication that tells you in advance what any genomic study can possibly find
lessons.description: The overlapping timescales of evolution and transmission, the substitutions-per-transmission calculation, and how to test whether a population is measurably evolving.
lessons.practical: For a pathogen you work on: find a published evolutionary rate, multiply by genome length and serial interval, and write the sentence 'sequencing this pathogen can distinguish ___ but cannot distinguish ___'.

quiz.question: A virus has an evolutionary rate of 1e-3 substitutions per site per year, a 10 kb genome and a 4-day serial interval. Roughly how many substitutions separate two people in a direct transmission?
options: About 0.01
About 1.1
About 4.0
About 0.1
quiz.explanation: 1e-3 x 10,000 = 10 substitutions per genome per year. Multiplied by 4/365 years gives about 0.11. At roughly one mutation per ten transmissions, this pathogen resolves lineages and introductions but cannot order individual links.

quiz.question: Why can mpox be used for outbreak-scale epidemiology despite orthopoxviruses having a baseline rate around 1e-6 per site per year?
options: Structural variants accumulate independently of the point substitution rate
Poxvirus polymerases progressively lose their proofreading capacity during sustained transmission in a human host
Its 197 kb genome is large enough that even a very low per-site rate yields many changes
Host APOBEC3 editing during human transmission drives an apparent rate far above baseline
quiz.explanation: APOBEC3 deaminates cytosine in single-stranded DNA, producing C-to-T changes fast enough to give a usable clock during human-to-human chains. Genome length alone does not rescue it: at baseline the rate is roughly 0.2 substitutions per genome per year.

quiz.question: The mutation rate and the substitution rate differ. What separates them?
options: The generation time of the pathogen, which is what converts a per-replication rate into a per-year rate
Sequencing error, which inflates observed differences above the true mutation rate
Selection and bottlenecks, which remove most mutations before they are ever observed
Genome length, since longer genomes present more sites at which a copying error can occur during each replication
quiz.explanation: The mutation rate is a property of the polymerase. The substitution rate is what survives purifying selection, population bottlenecks and your sampling — usually far less. Generation time and genome length are conversions between units, not the source of the gap.

quiz.question: A dataset's root-to-tip regression produces a flat, shapeless cloud. What follows?
options: Re-root the tree using midpoint rooting, which does not depend on temporal signal
The population is not measurably evolving over this window, so it cannot be dated
Increase the MCMC chain length and the number of recorded samples until the tMRCA credible interval narrows sufficiently
Fit an uncorrelated lognormal relaxed clock, since a shapeless root-to-tip cloud is the signature of rate variation between lineages
quiz.explanation: No temporal signal means no dating. The software will still return a tMRCA, but it will be the prior restated with a credible interval that looks like evidence. Neither a relaxed clock nor a longer chain creates signal that is absent from the data.

quiz.question: Influenza A's eight segments matter for genomic epidemiology because:
options: The segments must be concatenated before alignment, which introduces frameshift artefacts
Segmentation raises the effective per-site substitution rate, because each segment is replicated independently by its own polymerase complex
Each of the eight segments requires an independently designed tiling amplicon scheme in order to be sequenced
Reassortment means there is no single phylogeny, so one tree cannot describe the virus
quiz.explanation: Segments swap wholesale between co-infecting viruses, so influenza has eight phylogenies that can disagree. This is why H5N1 findings are expressed as genotypes — combinations of segment lineages — rather than as subtypes.

exercises.label: Conceptual
exercises.prompt: A colleague proposes sequencing to reconstruct who-infected-whom in a hepatitis B outbreak in a dialysis unit. Before looking at any data, what do you need to know, and what would make you say no?
exercises.guidance: You need the evolutionary rate, the genome length (~3.2 kb, which is small enough that rate × length is low) and the interval between infections. HBV is a slowly evolving DNA virus with a chronic course. Multiply and you will get well under one substitution per transmission, which rules out ordering individual links. Genomics can still exclude links and identify a common source, which in a dialysis unit is usually the question that matters.

exercises.label: Read the output
exercises.prompt: A root-to-tip regression, as TempEst reports it. Answer the three questions.
exercises.output:
Dataset A                          Dataset B
  slope      8.1e-4 subs/site/yr     slope      -2.0e-5 subs/site/yr
  x-intercept 2026-02-19             x-intercept 1974-06-03
  correlation 0.86                   correlation 0.04
  R-squared   0.74                   R-squared   0.002
  residual mean sq 1.1e-8            residual mean sq 9.4e-7
  tips 525                           tips 61
questions: For dataset A, what do the slope and the x-intercept each estimate?
Dataset B was run through the same pipeline and produced a tMRCA with a tight credible interval. Should you believe it?
What is the one thing the correlation coefficient here does NOT justify, given how the points were generated?
exercises.guidance: A: the slope estimates the evolutionary rate in substitutions per site per year; the x-intercept estimates the date of the root. B: no — a near-zero slope, a correlation of 0.04 and an x-intercept fifty years before sampling are the signature of no temporal signal. The software still returned a tMRCA, and that tMRCA is the prior restated with a credible interval that looks like evidence. Third: the tips share ancestry, so they are not independent observations; the correlation is a diagnostic that dating is possible, not a significance test, and ordinary least squares understates the uncertainty.

exercises.label: Three of six
exercises.prompt: Exactly three of these statements are correct.

statements.text: The substitution rate is lower than the mutation rate because selection and bottlenecks remove most mutations before they are observed.
A pathogen with 0.05 substitutions per transmission can resolve individual transmission links given sufficient sequencing depth.
Coronaviruses evolve more slowly per site than influenza partly because they carry a proofreading exonuclease.
Influenza reassortment means a single phylogeny cannot describe the whole virus.
If a root-to-tip regression shows no temporal signal, using a relaxed clock will recover the ability to date the tree.
Evolutionary rates quoted per site per year are directly comparable between pathogens without reference to genome length.

exercises.guidance: 1, 3 and 4. Depth cannot create mutations that never happened; a relaxed clock accommodates rate variation but does not manufacture signal; and a per-site rate must be multiplied by genome length before two pathogens can be compared — the same rate on a 30 kb and a 3 kb genome gives tenfold different resolution.

exercises.label: Scaffolded
exercises.prompt: The arithmetic is set out below with one step missing for each pathogen. Complete it, then write the resolution verdict.

exercises.guidance: SARS-CoV-2: 23.9 per year, 0.33 per transmission. Measles: 9.5 per year, 0.37. TB: 0.4 × 550/365 = 0.60. All three sit in the productive 0.3–0.7 band, which is why clusters resolve and individual links do not — and note that TB gets there by a completely different route, a very slow clock against a very long serial interval.

lessons.title: Mutation, substitution, signal, artefact
lessons.subtitle: The vocabulary that stops you being fooled, and the host enzymes that write fake mutations
lessons.description: Precise terminology for genetic change, why the consensus genome discards within-host diversity, and how to recognise APOBEC3, ADAR and oxidative signatures from base-change patterns alone.
lessons.practical: Take a phylodynamic paper on an RNA virus. How many sequences were generated versus analysed, was mutational-signature screening done, was outlier removal iterative, and was the alignment trimmed with a stated reason?

quiz.question: A filovirus genome shows an excess of T-to-C changes concentrated in short consecutive runs. What is the most likely explanation?
options: APOBEC3 editing, whose signature is cytosine deamination occurring in exposed single-stranded regions of the genome
Primer sequence retained in the consensus because trimming was omitted
Oxidative damage introduced while shearing the sample during library preparation, which is characteristically strand-biased
ADAR host editing, which is processive and therefore affects short spans
quiz.explanation: ADAR deaminates adenosine in double-stranded RNA and works processively, so the marks cluster. APOBEC3 acts on ssDNA and writes C-to-T; oxidative damage writes G-to-T; retained primer sequence produces reversions to reference, not runs of T-to-C.

quiz.question: Why does a consensus genome make a mixed infection hard to detect?
options: It reports the majority base per position, so a minor lineage is averaged away or lost
Ambiguity codes are not permitted in FASTA, so mixtures must be resolved arbitrarily
Mixed infections raise the overall per-position error rate above the consensus frequency threshold used by the pipeline
Reads from the two lineages map to overlapping positions and are discarded by the pipeline as ambiguous duplicates
quiz.explanation: Consensus calling is a majority summary of a within-host population. Two lineages either average into one impossible sequence or the minor one falls below threshold. Detecting mixture requires the reads, which is why archiving only FASTA forecloses the question permanently.

quiz.question: The Bundibugyo team removed root-to-tip outliers iteratively rather than in one pass. Why?
options: Single-pass removal becomes computationally more expensive than iteration once the tree exceeds a few hundred tips
Editing on an internal branch affects multiple tips, so outliers are not independent
A convention in the field requires at least two rounds before reporting a clock rate
Iterating allows the substitution model to be re-selected as sequences are removed
quiz.explanation: A bout of ADAR editing on an internal branch propagates to every descendant tip. Treating those tips as independent outliers and removing them in one pass under-corrects; re-rooting and re-fitting between rounds handles the dependency.

quiz.question: Which exclusion practice makes a phylodynamic analysis most defensible?
options: Removing sequences one at a time until the root-to-tip regression reaches an acceptable R-squared, then reporting that final fit
Applying a mechanistic filter first, reporting counts at every stage, and iterating
Excluding every sequence falling below the median genome completeness value calculated for the dataset as a whole
Retaining every sequence and correcting for artefacts within the substitution model
quiz.explanation: The mechanistic filter removes sequences for a stated biological reason before the blunt statistical filter runs, counts let a reader reconstruct what happened, and iteration handles non-independence. Removing sequences until the fit improves is fitting the filter to the desired result.

quiz.question: Why is a change at the very end of a viral genome treated with suspicion?
options: Terminal regions of the genome evolve faster and therefore saturate, which makes changes there uninformative about ancestry
Alignment algorithms systematically insert gaps at sequence termini, so terminal positions are unreliable in every dataset
Reverse transcription initiates at the 3-prime end and introduces characteristic errors
Coverage falls off and primers sit there, so assembly is ragged and artefacts concentrate
quiz.explanation: Genome ends are where depth drops, primer sequence sits and assemblers produce ragged output. This is why the Bundibugyo alignment was trimmed to 18,900 bases after one genome showed end artefacts — losing a few positions everywhere to remove noise contaminating all of it.

exercises.label: Conceptual
exercises.prompt: Your programme archives consensus FASTA files only, to save storage. Name three questions that decision makes permanently unanswerable, and one it does not affect.
exercises.guidance: Foreclosed: mixed infection, minority resistant subpopulations, and the transmission bottleneck — all need reads. Unaffected: lineage reassignment when a nomenclature scheme is revised, which works fine from FASTA. The point is that this is a policy decision usually made by default and regretted later.

exercises.label: Read the output
exercises.prompt: A screening script reports the base-change spectrum for four genomes against the outbreak consensus.
questions: Which genome shows a host editing signature, which one, and what in the table is the decisive clue rather than the base change alone?
26FHV118 shows 11 G>T changes. What is the most likely source, and is it the patient, the pathogen or the laboratory?
26FHV203 has no unusual spectrum. Should it enter the phylodynamic analysis?
exercises.guidance: 26FHV054 is ADAR: T>C is the signature on the strand filovirus genomes are written on, but the decisive clue is `runs_of_>=3` — ADAR is processive and edits short consecutive spans, which is what distinguishes it from ordinary substitution. 26FHV118 is oxidative damage from library preparation — the laboratory’s own signature, not the patient’s and not the virus’s. 26FHV203 is spectrally normal but 31% N: it will fail a completeness threshold, and that exclusion is a load-load-dependent one that removes late presenters and remote health zones preferentially.

exercises.label: Three of six
exercises.prompt: Exactly three of these statements are correct.

statements.text: APOBEC3 and ADAR both impose mutations that are host-derived rather than replication error.
A consensus base can change between two serial samples from one patient without the within-host population changing.
Iterative outlier removal is used because it converges faster than single-pass removal.
Homopolymer indels are more suspicious on nanopore data than on Illumina data.
Trimming an alignment removes artefactual signal at no cost to real signal.
Excluding sequences is defensible as long as the final root-to-tip regression fits well.

exercises.guidance: 1, 2 and 4. Iteration is used because editing on an internal branch affects multiple tips, so outliers are not independent — not for speed. Trimming removes positions from every sequence, including those with no artefact there. And removing sequences until the fit improves is fitting the filter to the desired result; the criterion has to be stated before the outcome.

exercises.label: Scaffolded
exercises.prompt: The exclusion cascade below is missing its reasons. Fill each in, then say which of the two filters should run first and why.
exercises.guidance: 32 removed for ADAR editing signatures — a mechanistic filter, justified by a known biological process with a known signature. 69 removed as root-to-tip outliers beyond ±2 SD, applied iteratively — a statistical filter. The mechanistic one runs first, because it removes sequences for a stated reason and leaves the blunt statistical filter with less to do; run the other way round, the statistical filter absorbs the edited genomes and you never learn why they were odd.

lessons.title: Sample to library — the wet-lab chain and the decisions inside it that are epidemiological
lessons.subtitle: The Ct threshold is a sampling frame wearing laboratory clothes
lessons.description: Specimen choice, extraction, the Ct gate and the selection it introduces, the four enrichment strategies, multiplexing and the controls that must be on every run.
lessons.practical: Find a methods section and extract: specimen types, the sequencing selection rule, enrichment strategy and primer scheme version, whether primer trimming is mentioned, and the controls. Then write one sentence describing the sampling frame.

quiz.question: Sequencing all PCR-positive samples with Ct below 31 is described as an epidemiological decision. Why?
options: Because it introduces a fixed false-negative rate into the workflow that must be corrected for in any prevalence estimate
Because Ct thresholds differ between assays and cannot be compared across laboratories
Because samples falling above the threshold are still sequenced, but only ever at substantially reduced genome coverage
Because viral load tracks onset timing, severity and access to care, so the gate selects cases
quiz.explanation: The threshold is correct laboratory practice and simultaneously a sampling frame. It enriches for people who presented early and sick, and because access to care varies geographically, it structures the genomic sample in exactly the dimension phylogeography tries to estimate.

quiz.question: A tiling amplicon scheme's primer binding site acquires a mutation in the circulating virus. What are the two consequences?
options: Formation of chimeric amplicons spanning two primer pools, and a systematic underestimation of the true genome length
Loss of strand balance, and elevated homopolymer indel rates in the affected amplicon
Increased yield for that amplicon, and a corresponding overrepresentation of the affected region in the coverage profile
Amplicon dropout producing Ns, and a false reversion to reference if primers are not trimmed
quiz.explanation: A mismatched primer amplifies poorly, so you lose coverage exactly where the virus changed. And if primer sequence reaches the consensus untrimmed, it contributes the reference base at the variable position — manufacturing a reversion.

quiz.question: An outbreak presents as an unknown illness with high mortality and no candidate pathogen. Which enrichment approach is indicated?
options: Metagenomic shotgun sequencing, because it requires no prior knowledge of the target
Tiling amplicon PCR, because it is most sensitive at high Ct values
Culture followed by whole genome sequencing, because it yields abundant clean nucleic acid
Bait capture with a broad viral family panel, because probes tolerate divergence
quiz.explanation: Only metagenomics can find something nobody hypothesised. Amplicons need primers, which need a known target; capture needs probes, which need a panel; culture needs something that grows. Metagenomics costs far more and is less sensitive, which is the price of the agnosticism.

quiz.question: Why should an outbreak sequencing run's positive control be a distinguishable strain?
options: To calibrate the relationship between Ct value and achieved genome coverage for the specific assay in use
So that contamination of a sample by the control can be detected rather than hidden
To provide a reference for depth normalisation across barcodes within the run
To satisfy laboratory accreditation requirements for full traceability of control materials used in each diagnostic run
quiz.explanation: If the control is the same strain as the outbreak, contamination is invisible — the contaminated sample simply looks like a case. A distinguishable control turns a silent failure into a detectable one.

quiz.question: What most often dominates sample-to-answer time in outbreak sequencing?
options: Phylogenetic analysis, since Bayesian inference requires long MCMC chains
Transport of the specimen and waiting to fill a flow cell
Basecalling on under-provisioned compute, since super-accurate nanopore models require a GPU that field laboratories rarely have
Library preparation, which involves several enzymatic steps including at least one overnight incubation
quiz.explanation: Logistics and batching dominate. The run itself is rarely the bottleneck, which is why decentralised sequencing and small frequent batches — not faster chemistry — are what improve outbreak turnaround.

exercises.label: Conceptual
exercises.prompt: An outbreak presents as “unknown severe illness, high mortality” with no candidate pathogen. Rank the four enrichment strategies for this situation and justify the ranking in one sentence each.
exercises.guidance: Metagenomics first — it is the only one that can find something nobody hypothesised. Capture second, if a broad viral-family panel plausibly covers it. Culture third, and only for what grows. Amplicon last and effectively unusable, because it needs primers, which need a known target. Once the agent is identified the ranking inverts completely, which is the point.

exercises.label: Read the output
exercises.prompt: A sequencing run manifest from a field laboratory. Answer the three questions.
questions: Which sample would a Ct < 31 selection rule have excluded, and which would a 90% coverage rule exclude? Are they the same sample?
Something on this run needs investigating before any of these consensus sequences are used. What, and what does it threaten?
S-043 and S-044 are oral fluid from deceased patients. What does losing them do to the epidemiology, beyond losing two data points?
exercises.guidance: Ct < 31 excludes S-044 only. The 90% coverage rule excludes both S-043 and S-044 — so the two filters are not the same, and they compound. The urgent problem is NEG-B: 44,000 reads and 6% genome coverage in a no-template control means contamination or index hopping in pool B, which threatens exactly the Q1 linkage claims that would make two samples look identical. Losing the oral-fluid samples removes people who died in the community — the group most likely to sit in undetected chains — so the loss is structured, not random.

exercises.label: Three of six
exercises.prompt: Exactly three of these statements are correct.

statements.text: Ct values are comparable across laboratories provided the same target gene is used.
A mutation under a primer binding site causes loss of coverage precisely where the pathogen changed.
Bait capture tolerates a divergent target better than tiling amplicon PCR does.
Multiplexing reduces the marginal cost per genome and simultaneously creates the main cross-contamination risk.
A positive control identical to the outbreak strain is preferable because it validates the whole workflow.
Metagenomics is more sensitive than amplicon PCR for a known target at high Ct.

exercises.guidance: 2, 3 and 4. Ct depends on assay, extraction volume, instrument and threshold setting, so it is an internally consistent ordering within one workflow and nothing more. An identical positive control makes contamination of a sample by the control invisible. And metagenomics is markedly less sensitive than targeted amplification at low template.

exercises.label: Scaffolded
exercises.prompt: Complete the tiling scheme diagram, then answer what breaks.
exercises.output:
genome  ─────────────────────────────────────────────

pool 1  ▔▔▔▔▔▔▔      ▔▔▔▔▔▔▔      ▔▔▔▔▔▔▔      ▔▔▔▔▔▔▔

Q1  Why are neighbouring amplicons never in the same pool?
Q2  Why must the amplicons overlap rather than abut?
Q3  A mutation appears under a pool-1 primer. Which two things go wrong?
exercises.guidance: Q1: overlapping products in one reaction amplify each other and produce short junk. Q2: abutting amplicons leave gaps at every junction once the ends are trimmed. Q3: amplicon dropout, giving a run of Ns exactly where the virus changed; and, if primer sequence is not trimmed from the reads, the primer’s reference base is called as consensus — a manufactured reversion to reference at the variable site.

lessons.title: The machines — how DNA becomes data
lessons.subtitle: Basecalling is the literal moment a molecule becomes a file, and its version belongs in your metadata
lessons.description: Illumina sequencing-by-synthesis and nanopore mechanism, Phred scores and why depth beats per-read accuracy, adaptive sampling, and platform choice as a surveillance-design decision.
lessons.practical: For a surveillance programme you know: write down samples arriving per week, acceptable sample-to-answer time, genome size and repeat structure, and available power/cold chain/compute/maintenance. Then pick a platform and answer: what happens the day the machine breaks?

quiz.question: Nanopore reads had per-base accuracy well below Illumina's for years, yet produced reliable consensus genomes. Why?
options: Errors are largely independent between reads, so depth converts poor reads into a good consensus
Consensus calling applies a platform-specific error model that corrects the systematic biases characteristic of nanopore chemistry
Amplicon sequencing avoids the genomic regions where nanopore error rates are highest
Nanopore reads are much longer, so each individual read spans many more informative sites than a short read does
quiz.explanation: With random, independent errors, the chance that a majority of 100 reads agree on the same wrong base is negligible. This is why minimum-depth thresholds are the load-bearing quality control rather than per-read quality — and why systematic error, which depth cannot fix, is the real hazard.

quiz.question: Why does the basecaller version belong in a sequence's metadata?
options: Because it determines the maximum read length the instrument can produce
Because re-basecalling the same raw signal with a newer model yields different sequence
Because different basecaller versions support different flow cell chemistries and sequencing kit combinations
Because regulatory accreditation of a clinical sequencing service requires traceability of every software version in the workflow
quiz.explanation: Basecalling is a model, and models have versions. Genomes compared across basecaller versions differ partly because of software rather than biology. This is the same reproducibility argument that makes pipeline version pinning worth the effort.

quiz.question: What does nanopore adaptive sampling do?
options: Varies the applied voltage across the membrane to enrich for longer fragments
Reads the start of a molecule, then ejects it if uninteresting, freeing the pore
Adjusts the speed at which the motor protein ratchets the strand through the pore, trading accuracy against throughput
Selects which barcoded samples to basecall first, based on how coverage is accumulating across the run in real time
quiz.explanation: Because the pore can be electrically reversed, the software can reject a read after seeing its first few hundred bases. This gives host depletion and targeted enrichment in software rather than at the bench — valuable for low-biomass, high-host metagenomic samples.

quiz.question: A national laboratory receives 15 samples a week in bursts, has unreliable power, no service engineer nearby, and needs results within 72 hours. What is the strongest argument against buying a high-throughput short-read instrument?
options: Reagent kits for high-throughput platforms have shorter shelf lives
High-throughput instruments are only efficient when saturated, so batching adds fatal latency
Short reads cannot span repetitive regions, so bacterial assemblies fragment into contigs rather than closing into a chromosome
Per-base accuracy becomes largely irrelevant once consensus depth across the genome is adequate
quiz.explanation: The instrument is efficient only when filled. At 15 samples a week, filling it means waiting, and waiting destroys the 72-hour requirement that justified the purchase. Match the instrument to the arrival rate, not to the annual total.

quiz.question: A variant is seen only on one sequencing platform and never on the other. What should you suspect?
options: Insufficient depth on the platform where it was not observed
A genuine minority variant below the second platform's consensus threshold
Systematic error specific to that platform's chemistry or basecaller
Index hopping between barcodes within the run where it appeared
quiz.explanation: Random error is beaten by depth; systematic error is not, because every read is wrong identically. Platform-specific weaknesses — homopolymer length on nanopore, particular sequence contexts on Illumina — are the first explanation for a platform-specific variant.

exercises.label: Conceptual
exercises.prompt: A national laboratory receives 15 samples a week in unpredictable bursts, has intermittent mains power, no service engineer within 2,000 km, and needs results in 72 hours. Argue for a platform, then answer: what happens the day the machine breaks?
exercises.guidance: Nanopore, amplicon, on site. The instrument is cheap enough to hold a spare, runs off a laptop, tolerates the power situation, produces output in real time and works in small frequent batches. A high-throughput short-read instrument is efficient only when saturated, and at 15 samples a week saturating it means batching, which destroys the 72-hour requirement that justified buying it. The breakage question is the one that decides it: a $1,000 device you can replace beats a $300,000 device that becomes a cupboard.

Errors are largely independent between reads, so at adequate depth the chance that a majority agree on the same wrong base is negligible — depth converts mediocre reads into an excellent consensus, and minimum-depth thresholds rather than read quality are the load-bearing control. The two metadata fields are the basecaller version and model, and the chemistry/kit: re-basecalling the same raw signal with a newer model produces different sequence, so genomes compared across versions differ partly because of software rather than biology. The tight ~1,200 b distribution says this is an amplicon library with a ~1,200 b scheme; a broad distribution would indicate metagenomic or native DNA input.

statements.text: Depth compensates for random per-read error but not for systematic error.
Adaptive sampling gives host depletion without additional wet-lab work.
Illumina's dominant error mode is the indel; nanopore's is the substitution.
Basecalling a nanopore run with a super-accurate model typically needs a GPU.
A variant seen on only one of two platforms is most likely a real minority variant.
PacBio HiFi is the appropriate default for routine national viral surveillance.

exercises.guidance: 1, 2 and 4. The error modes are the other way round — Illumina makes substitutions, nanopore historically made indels in homopolymers. A platform-specific variant should first be suspected of being that platform’s systematic error. And PacBio’s cost keeps it out of routine surveillance, whatever its accuracy.

Illumina: you need per-base accuracy at 0–5 SNP resolution and at volume, and weekly batching is acceptable against a 2–3 week requirement. Add long reads selectively to close plasmids, which short reads cannot span.

lessons.title: Reads to genome — the bioinformatics chain and the four thresholds that decide your dataset
lessons.subtitle: Four numbers set by humans, all pushing the same way
lessons.description: File formats and what each discards, mapping versus assembly, primer trimming, depth and breadth, and the compound selection produced by the four QC thresholds.
topics: FASTQ to BAM to VCF to FASTA
lessons.practical: Open a methods section and find the pipeline version, minimum depth, completeness threshold, primer trimming and the sample counts at each stage. Then draw the cascade from cases to analysed genomes.

quiz.question: A surveillance programme archives only consensus FASTA files. What is permanently foreclosed?
options: Recalculation of pairwise SNP distances against a different reference genome
Construction of time-scaled phylogenies from the archived sequences at any point in the future
Retrospective analysis of within-host diversity, mixture and minority resistance
Re-assignment of lineages when a nomenclature scheme is revised
quiz.explanation: Consensus discards read-level information by construction. Lineage reassignment and distance recalculation work fine from FASTA; anything about the within-host population needs BAMs or FASTQs, and once discarded they cannot be regenerated.

quiz.question: Why is primer trimming not optional for amplicon-derived consensus genomes?
options: Retained primer sequence inflates the apparent genome length and biases the alignment trimming step downstream
Primers carry reference bases, so a mutation under a primer is called as a reversion
Retained primer sequence is read as adapter contamination and propagates into every downstream assembly and alignment
Untrimmed primers cause reads to fail mapping and reduce effective coverage
quiz.explanation: The primer was synthesised from the reference. If its bases reach the consensus, they overwrite the patient's actual base at exactly the variable position — manufacturing a reversion to reference where a real mutation exists.

quiz.question: The four QC thresholds in the bioinformatics chain share a structural problem. What is it?
options: They interact non-linearly, so their combined effect cannot be predicted
They are applied after lineage assignment, so lineage calls are made on rejected data
They are pathogen-specific and therefore cannot be compared between programmes working on different organisms
They all preferentially remove low-load samples, compounding the Ct gate's selection
quiz.explanation: Minimum depth, consensus frequency, maximum N fraction and outlier distance all push the same way: out go the samples with least material, which came disproportionately from late presenters, milder cases and remote areas. The Ct gate selected once; these select again in the same direction.

quiz.question: What is the fastest check that a suspicious genomic cluster is a laboratory artefact rather than transmission?
options: Rebuild the tree under a more parameter-rich substitution model and check whether the cluster persists
Colour the tree by sequencing batch and look for clustering by run
Recompute the alignment with a different multiple sequence aligner and check whether the cluster survives the change
Compare consensus sequences called at two different frequency thresholds
quiz.explanation: Contamination and index hopping produce shared spurious variants, and therefore a well-supported clade of samples that share nothing but a flow cell. Colouring by run takes a minute and has saved entire studies.

quiz.question: Depth and breadth of coverage differ how?
options: Depth is a per-sample average; breadth is a per-run average across the flow cell
Depth applies to mapped data; breadth applies only to de novo assemblies
Depth counts reads at a position; breadth is the fraction of the genome above a depth threshold
Depth is measured on raw reads before trimming, whereas breadth is measured on the final trimmed and primer-clipped alignment
quiz.explanation: Depth is per-position read count; breadth is genome completeness at a chosen depth. Amplicon data is typically spiky, so a single depth threshold applied across an uneven profile can mask entire amplicons while the average looks healthy.

exercises.label: Conceptual
exercises.prompt: Explain to a non-bioinformatician why a coverage hole in a viral genome is worse than a random gap of the same size.
exercises.guidance: Because it is not random. In amplicon data a hole usually means a mutation under a primer stopped that amplicon amplifying — so you lose data preferentially at the positions where the virus changed, which are the positions you most wanted. The missingness is informative and it points the wrong way.

exercises.label: Read the output
exercises.prompt: Per-amplicon depth for one sample, and the consensus summary.
questions: Amplicon 3 has failed. Give the most likely biological cause and say what it implies about that region.
‘primer trimming: NOT APPLIED’ — what specific error will appear in this consensus, and where?
This sample is 86.4% complete. A 90% threshold would drop it. Is dropping it the right call?
exercises.guidance: Amplicon 3 has almost certainly lost a primer binding site to a mutation — so the region that failed is likely the region that changed. Without primer trimming, the primer’s reference bases are called as consensus at the start and end of every surviving amplicon, producing false reversions to reference at exactly the variable primer-site positions. On the threshold: the honest answer is that it depends on the question. For lineage assignment 86% may be fine; for a linkage claim that turns on a position inside the dropout it is useless. A single global threshold applied without reference to the question is the thing to avoid — and either way the loss is not random.

exercises.label: Three of six
exercises.prompt: Exactly three of these statements are correct.

statements.text: BAM files retain within-host diversity that consensus FASTA has discarded.
Breadth of coverage is the number of reads at a given position.
Colouring a phylogeny by sequencing run is a fast test for contamination artefacts.
Reference mapping can reveal large insertions that are absent from the reference.
De novo assembly is generally necessary for bacteria because the accessory genome varies between isolates.
A pipeline version is a bureaucratic detail with no effect on the sequences produced.

exercises.guidance: 1, 3 and 5. Breadth is the fraction of the genome above a depth threshold; depth is the read count at a position. Mapping can only show you what maps, so large insertions absent from the reference are invisible or misassembled. And pipeline and basecaller versions demonstrably change the genomes you get.

Every arrow removes low-load, late-presenting, remote and milder cases preferentially, so the compound bias runs in one direction throughout: the analysed set over-represents people who presented early, severely, and close to a functioning laboratory.

lessons.title: Naming things — clades, lineages, variants, sequence types and the SNP threshold
lessons.subtitle: A name is a claim about a tree; a SNP threshold is a case definition
lessons.description: Four overlapping naming systems, Pango aliasing, influenza genotypes, MLST and cgMLST, and how to interrogate a SNP-threshold cluster definition.
lessons.practical: Take three news items about a 'new variant'. For each, identify the naming system, state what the name asserts phylogenetically, state the phenotypic claim being made, and note the gap between the two.

quiz.question: What does assigning a sequence to a Pango lineage assert?
options: That it carries the phenotypic properties epidemiologically associated with that lineage elsewhere
That it belongs to a defined clade on the phylogeny, and nothing more
That it is antigenically distinct from the parental lineage it descends from
That it has been designated by WHO as a variant of interest or concern
quiz.explanation: A lineage name is a statement about phylogenetic position. Phenotype, risk designation and antigenic distinctness are separate claims requiring separate evidence — and conflating naming with importance is how a designation becomes a headline.

quiz.question: Why is the H5N1 dairy cattle finding expressible only at genotype resolution?
options: A genotype names a combination of lineages across all eight reassorting segments
Subtype designations are revised too frequently to support an epidemiological claim that must remain stable over time
Genotypes are assigned from whole genome data whereas subtypes use serology
Clade 2.3.4.4b spans several host species, so the name cannot distinguish a cattle-adapted lineage from an avian one
quiz.explanation: H5N1 names two surface proteins and covers thousands of distinct viruses; clade 2.3.4.4b names a haemagglutinin clade only. The finding is about one specific reassortant and its descendants, and only the genotype name carries that.

quiz.question: A colleague proposes a 5-SNP threshold to define outbreak clusters. What is the first thing to ask?
options: What the background pairwise distance is among unlinked local isolates
Whether the threshold matches published values for this pathogen
Which alignment masking scheme will be applied before distances are computed
Whether single or complete linkage will be used to assemble clusters
quiz.explanation: A threshold is meaningless without the local background distribution. If unlinked isolates routinely sit 3 SNPs apart in this setting, a 5-SNP rule has terrible specificity. Linkage rule and masking matter too, but they are secondary to knowing what the number is being compared against.

quiz.question: Why is cgMLST allele-based rather than SNP-based?
options: Allele calling captures insertions and deletions, which reference-mapped SNP-based methods discard from the distance entirely
Allele profiles can be computed without a reference genome assembly
A single SNP and a recombined block both count as one difference, limiting recombination's inflation
Allele calling is computationally cheaper on large bacterial genome collections
quiz.explanation: Counting a whole recombined locus as one allele difference stops a single recombination event from contributing dozens of SNPs and shattering a real cluster. The cost is that schemes are only comparable within themselves.

quiz.question: Why does this course insist that Bundibugyo virus is not a variant of Ebola virus?
options: It is a distinct species, so vaccines and therapeutics for Zaire ebolavirus do not apply
Because filovirus taxonomy names species after the place of first detection rather than by phylogenetic position
Because variant designations are formally reserved for viruses currently under active WHO risk assessment
Because Bundibugyo virus has a segmented genome and Ebola virus does not
quiz.explanation: The distinction is taxonomic and it has consequences: ERVEBO and the licensed monoclonals target Zaire ebolavirus, and Bundibugyo is far enough away that cross-protection cannot be assumed. That is why there was no licensed countermeasure in the 2026 outbreak.

exercises.label: Conceptual
exercises.prompt: A press office asks you to approve the sentence “a dangerous new variant has been detected.” Rewrite it truthfully for a lineage that has been designated but not phenotypically characterised, and explain what you removed.
exercises.guidance: Something like: ‘a previously undesignated lineage has been detected; it is defined by its position on the phylogeny, and there is currently no evidence about its transmissibility, severity or effect on diagnostics.’ You removed ‘dangerous’, which is a phenotypic claim nobody has evidence for, and you replaced ‘variant’ with ‘lineage’, which says what was actually observed.

exercises.label: Read the output
exercises.prompt: Nextclade output for four sequences. Answer the three questions.
exercises.output:
seqName    clade    lineage    totalMutations  privateMutations  QC.overall  QC.flags
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
GS-0117    23F      XBB.1.5         41                3            good      —
GS-0118    23F      XBB.1.5         39                2            good      —
GS-0119    23F      XBB.1.5        118               71            bad       privateMutations; clusteredSNPs
GS-0120    ?        ?               12                9            bad       missingData (68.2% N)
questions: GS-0119 has 71 private mutations and clustered SNPs. Give two explanations, one biological and one technical, and say which you would investigate first.
GS-0120 could not be assigned. Is that a property of the virus or of the sample?
GS-0117 and GS-0118 differ by two mutations. What, if anything, does that say about a transmission link between those two cases?
exercises.guidance: Biological: a long unsampled chain, or a chronic infection in an immunocompromised host where within-host evolution accelerated. Technical: contamination, co-infection, or index hopping producing a mixture. Investigate the technical explanation first — it is far more common and it is cheap to check (negative controls, run assignment, allele frequencies at the private sites). GS-0120 is a sample problem: 68% N means insufficient template or a failed run, not an unusual virus. And two mutations between GS-0117 and GS-0118 says very little on its own; you need the local background distance distribution before that number carries any information.

exercises.label: Three of six
exercises.prompt: Exactly three of these statements are correct.

statements.text: A WHO variant label is a risk assessment rather than a phylogenetic designation.
cgMLST counts a single SNP and a whole recombined block each as one allele difference.
SNP distances are comparable between studies as long as both used whole genome sequencing.
Single-linkage clustering produces smaller, more conservative clusters than complete linkage.
Influenza requires a genotype rather than a subtype name because its segments reassort.
A serotype is a phylogenetic category.

exercises.guidance: 1, 2 and 5. SNP distances depend on the reference and the masking scheme, so they are not comparable across studies that chose differently. Single linkage chains clusters together and grows them without limit; complete linkage is the conservative one. And a serotype is a phenotype — an antigenic type originally read with antibodies, inferable from sequence but not defined by the tree.

exercises.label: Scaffolded
exercises.prompt: A cluster definition is given with two of its five components. Supply the missing three, then say what you would need in order to defend the threshold.
exercises.output:
“Cluster A comprises 14 isolates within 5 SNPs of one another.”

  metric ......... SNP distance from a mapped alignment  ✓
  threshold ...... 5 SNPs  ✓
  linkage rule ... ______________________
  time window .... ______________________
  background ..... ______________________

  To defend the threshold I would need: ______________________
exercises.guidance: Linkage rule: single or complete — unstated in almost every published definition and it materially changes cluster size. Time window: without one, a 2018 and a 2026 isolate 4 SNPs apart will cluster, which is informative about a persistent lineage and not about current transmission. Background: the pairwise distance distribution among contemporaneous unlinked local isolates, without which the threshold carries no information. To defend it you need validation against epidemiologically confirmed links, with sensitivity and specificity reported — which is what almost nobody has.

lessons.phase_title: From data to trees to time
lessons.title: What a phylogenetic tree is, and the five things people read into it that are not there
lessons.subtitle: The transmission tree is not the phylogenetic tree, and three mechanisms keep them apart
lessons.description: Alignment as a hypothesis, the anatomy of a tree, the five standard misreadings, and why sequencing dismisses transmission links better than it confirms them.
lessons.practical: Open a Nextstrain build. Switch between time and divergence trees; colour by country then by originating lab; find a clade and ask whether it is large because of transmission or sampling.

quiz.question: Two tips are drawn adjacent on a published tree. What does that tell you about their relatedness?
options: They were sampled at similar times, provided the tree being shown is time-scaled rather than a divergence tree
They are sister taxa, unless the node immediately joining them is drawn as an unresolved polytomy
They share a recent common ancestor relative to the rest of the tree
Nothing — a tree can be rotated at any node without changing its meaning
quiz.explanation: Vertical position is a drawing convention and any node can be rotated freely. Only branching structure and branch lengths carry information; two tips can be adjacent on the page and separated by the deepest split in the tree.

quiz.question: Which mechanism does NOT contribute to the phylogenetic tree differing from the transmission tree?
options: Within-host diversity, so lineages diverge inside a donor before transmission
Substitution model misspecification biasing the estimated branch lengths
Too few mutations per transmission to order the links that did occur
Incomplete sampling leaving most transmission events unrepresented
quiz.explanation: Model misspecification degrades a tree's accuracy but is not what separates a tree of sequences from a tree of people. The three mechanisms are structural: sparse sampling, the pre-transmission interval created by within-host diversity, and insufficient mutation per link.

quiz.question: Why did the Bundibugyo authors collapse near-zero-length branches into polytomies?
options: To speed convergence of the MCMC chain by shrinking the tree space searched
To satisfy the assumption of bifurcation required by coalescent tree priors
To reduce the number of free parameters that the substitution model is required to estimate from the alignment
Because a fully bifurcating tree built from zero-length branches claims precision it lacks
quiz.explanation: At about 0.66 substitutions per transmission, many internal branches rest on no evidence at all. Drawing them as resolved bifurcations asserts an ordering the data never recorded. A polytomy is an honest statement that the order is unresolved.

quiz.question: An internal node in an outbreak phylogeny most likely corresponds to:
options: A reference genome included to anchor the alignment
The index case, if the tree is correctly rooted
The earliest sampled case within that clade
An inferred ancestral sequence from an unsampled infection
quiz.explanation: Internal nodes are inferred ancestors, not observations. Even a genuinely sampled ancestor appears as a tip with a short branch. With a small fraction of cases sequenced, essentially every internal node is someone you never sequenced.

quiz.question: Trimming an alignment to remove end-of-genome artefacts involves what trade?
options: Losing real signal from every sequence to remove artefactual signal from a few
Losing all indel information in exchange for more reliable substitution calls across the remaining positions
Reducing the number of alignment columns, and therefore the computational cost of every likelihood evaluation during the tree search
Discarding low-coverage samples in exchange for a more complete alignment
quiz.explanation: Trimming removes positions from all sequences, including the ones with no artefact there. It is the right call when artefacts concentrate at the edges — which for amplicon-derived viral genomes they reliably do — and the wrong call if it takes the informative sites too.

exercises.label: Conceptual
exercises.prompt: A colleague points at two tips adjacent on a printed tree and says “these two must be linked — look how close they are.” Give the shortest correct correction, then the longer one.
exercises.guidance: Short: vertical position is a drawing convention; the tree can be rotated at any node without changing its meaning, so adjacency on the page carries no information. Longer: what carries information is the branching structure and the branch lengths, and even those give a tree of sequences rather than a tree of people — so ‘linked’ needs the local background distance and, ideally, epidemiological evidence.

exercises.label: Read the output
exercises.prompt: A tree figure legend, exactly as submitted with a manuscript. Answer the three questions.
exercises.output:
Figure 2. Maximum likelihood phylogeny of 214 genomes from the outbreak
(IQ-TREE, GTR+F+G4). Tips coloured by health zone. Node support shown for
selected nodes. Tree midpoint-rooted. Scale bar omitted for clarity.

  Health zone   n sequenced   n cases reported
  Bunia               141            612
  Rwampara             48            409
  Mongbwalu            21            755
  Other (18 HZ)         4          1,972
questions: Two things in the legend should stop you drawing any quantitative conclusion from the figure. What are they?
The largest clade in the figure is from Bunia. What are the two competing explanations, and which does the table favour?
The tree is midpoint-rooted. What does that assume, and is the assumption reasonable here?
exercises.guidance: ‘Scale bar omitted’ means you cannot read branch lengths at all, so you cannot tell a divergence tree from a cladogram or judge any distance; and ‘support shown for selected nodes’ means support was reported where it was good. On the clade: intense Bunia transmission, or intense Bunia sequencing. Sequences per case are Bunia 0.23, Rwampara 0.12, Mongbwalu 0.03, elsewhere 0.002 — a hundredfold range, so sampling is the leading explanation and the figure cannot separate them. Midpoint rooting assumes a roughly constant rate across lineages; for a densely sampled time-stamped outbreak the defensible choice is clock-based rooting that minimises root-to-tip residuals.

exercises.label: Three of six
exercises.prompt: Exactly three of these statements are correct.

statements.text: A multiple sequence alignment is a hypothesis of homology, not an observation.
Internal nodes in an outbreak phylogeny usually correspond to sampled index cases.
A polytomy can be an honest statement that the data cannot resolve the branching order.
Within-host diversity means lineages can diverge before the transmission event that separates two hosts.
With perfect sampling, the phylogenetic tree becomes the transmission tree.
Ladderised trees show an evolutionary progression from primitive to derived tips.

exercises.guidance: 1, 3 and 4. Internal nodes are inferred ancestors, overwhelmingly from unsampled infections. Even perfect sampling would not make the two trees identical — the pre-transmission interval and the shortage of mutations per link both remain. And ladderisation is a layout choice; all tips are contemporary with their sampling dates and none is ancestral to another.

Item 5 is the one to ask for first anyway, because without sequences-per-case by health zone the geographic pattern may be entirely a sampling pattern, and that undermines the figure regardless of support. Item 6 matters because a fully bifurcating tree drawn from branches resting on a single mutation claims precision the data do not contain. Note also that rooting on a 2012 isolate is decades of divergence, which can distort branch lengths across the whole tree.

lessons.phase_title: From data to trees to time
lessons.title: Building the tree — substitution models, likelihood, support and rooting
lessons.subtitle: By the end, GTR+F+R3 is transparent and rooting is visibly a decision about the direction of time
lessons.description: Decoding model strings, why maximum likelihood is standard, how to read bootstrap and UFBoot support, the three rooting strategies, and the three ways a tree can be confidently wrong.
lessons.practical: For a published ML tree: what model and was it selected by procedure, what support metric and on what scale, how was it rooted and was a reason given, were near-zero branches collapsed, and was recombination screened for?

quiz.question: In GTR+F+R3, what does +R3 specify?
options: A three-parameter rate matrix restricting the six substitution types
Three freely-estimated site-rate classes, with no assumed rate distribution
Three independent MCMC replicate runs combined after burn-in
Three partitions corresponding to codon positions in coding regions
quiz.explanation: FreeRate estimates k rate categories and their weights directly from the data, unlike the more common +G gamma model which assumes a distributional shape governed by one parameter. R3 means three such classes.

quiz.question: An ultrafast bootstrap value of 78% on a branch should be read as:
options: Equivalent to a Bayesian posterior clade probability of approximately 0.78 for that same split
Not well supported, because UFBoot is read on a scale where 95% is the threshold
Uninterpretable on its own, because ultrafast bootstrap is only meaningful when reported alongside an SH-aLRT branch test
Well supported, since it exceeds the conventional 70% bootstrap threshold
quiz.explanation: UFBoot values are less biased than classical bootstrap and are conventionally read with 95% as the threshold for well supported. Applying the classical 70% cutoff to UFBoot systematically overstates confidence.

quiz.question: Why is residual-minimising rooting appropriate for a densely sampled single-outbreak dataset?
options: There is usually no suitable outgroup, and it uses the temporal signal that is present
It requires no assumption that substitution rates are constant across lineages, unlike every alternative rooting strategy
It is the only rooting strategy that is formally compatible with a time-reversible substitution model
It produces the shortest total tree length and is therefore most parsimonious
quiz.explanation: An earlier outbreak genome is decades divergent and distorts branch lengths; midpoint rooting assumes rate constancy. Clock-based rooting exploits what a time-stamped outbreak actually has — sampling dates — by choosing the root that best fits a root-to-tip regression.

quiz.question: A tree clusters samples by sequencing run rather than by geography or date, with high bootstrap support. What is happening?
options: Contamination or index hopping producing shared spurious variants
Genuine transmission within the facilities that submitted each batch
Rate variation between batches requiring a relaxed clock model
Alignment error concentrated in samples processed together
quiz.explanation: Shared contaminating reads really are shared, so the clade is well supported and completely artefactual. High support means your data under your model recover a split consistently — it says nothing about whether the data are real.

quiz.question: Recombination breaks maximum likelihood phylogenetics because:
options: Recombinant sequences cannot be aligned without inserting so many gaps that the homology hypothesis becomes untenable
Recombination rates cannot be estimated jointly with substitution rates in a single likelihood framework
Different genomic regions have different histories, so no single tree describes the alignment
It creates homoplasy that inflates bootstrap support beyond its nominal meaning
quiz.explanation: The whole framework assumes one tree for the whole alignment. Forcing one tree onto regions with different histories yields a tree that is wrong everywhere and often well supported — hence Gubbins and ClonalFrameML for bacteria, and per-segment trees for influenza.

exercises.label: Conceptual
exercises.prompt: Why does an observed count of differences underestimate evolutionary distance, and why does that matter much less for a 100-day outbreak than for a cross-species comparison?
exercises.guidance: Multiple hits: a site that changed and changed back reads as no change, and two independent identical changes read as no difference. The longer the elapsed time, the worse the underestimate, until distance saturates. Over 100 days on one virus, almost no site has been hit twice, so the correction is small — which is why the substitution model matters far less in outbreak analysis than in deep phylogenetics, without ever being nothing.

  GTR+F+R3      -28114.902   BIC  56701.55
  GTR+F+G4      -28129.771   BIC  56717.29

questions: Read the rate parameters. What general feature of DNA substitution do they show, and which two entries carry it?
The three site-rate classes are given as (proportion, rate). Describe the alignment they imply in one sentence.

The rate classes say 61% of sites are nearly invariant (rate 0.088), 31% evolve at about the average, and 8% evolve about seven times faster than average: a mostly-constrained genome with a small fast-evolving minority, which is exactly what +R3 is for and what a single gamma shape parameter would fit less well. And 47/213 is not a problem with the analysis — at well under one substitution per transmission, most internal branches rest on no evidence, so poor support is the honest resolution limit. The correct response is to collapse those branches, not to argue from their fine structure.

exercises.label: Three of six
exercises.prompt: Exactly three of these statements are correct.

statements.text: GTR allows a separate rate for each of the six reversible base-change types.
An ultrafast bootstrap value of 80% indicates a well-supported branch.
+F takes base frequencies from the alignment rather than estimating them as free parameters.
High bootstrap support indicates the substitution model was correctly specified.
Recombination can produce a tree that is both strongly supported and wrong everywhere.
Likelihood under a time-reversible model returns a rooted tree.

exercises.guidance: 1, 3 and 5. UFBoot is read at 95%. Support says how consistently your data under your model recover a split — nothing about whether the model, alignment or sampling is right. And time-reversibility is precisely why likelihood returns an unrooted tree; rooting is a separate decision.

exercises.label: Scaffolded
exercises.prompt: Decode the model string component by component, then say what the alternative to the last component would have assumed.
exercises.guidance: GTR: all six reversible base-change types have free rates. +F: base frequencies taken empirically from the alignment. +R3: FreeRate site-rate heterogeneity with three freely estimated rate classes and their proportions. +G4 assumes rates follow a gamma distribution, discretised into four categories governed by a single shape parameter — a stronger assumption about the shape of the rate distribution, which +R does not make.

lessons.title: Putting time on the tree — molecular clocks, tMRCA, and what a date of origin actually is
lessons.subtitle: The most over-interpreted number in the field, read correctly
lessons.description: Testing temporal signal, strict versus relaxed clocks, the three things tMRCA is not, and how to read ESS, burn-in and HPD intervals in a Bayesian phylodynamic result.
lessons.practical: For a time-scaled tree in your field: find the root-to-tip regression, the clock model, the tMRCA and its HPD, and ESS. Then compare the tMRCA with the date of first detection — that gap is the surveillance system's blind period.

quiz.question: A tMRCA of 22 February 2026 is estimated for an outbreak whose first case was recognised on 24 April. What does this establish?
options: The spillover from the animal reservoir into humans occurred on or very close to 22 February
Transmission among sequenced cases was established at least six to eight weeks before recognition
Surveillance sensitivity in the affected province was approximately 40% during that period
The index case was infected in late February and went undetected until the Bunia case was identified two months later
quiz.explanation: tMRCA is a lower bound on the age of the outbreak, conditional on the sequences you have. It is not the index case, not the spillover date, and it says nothing directly about surveillance sensitivity — only that the detection lag was at least this long.

quiz.question: Why does a tMRCA move when you add sequences?
options: MCMC chains require proportionally more steps as tip number grows
It is the ancestor of your sample, so an earlier divergent lineage pulls it back
Adding sequences changes which substitution model is selected by the information criterion, and therefore the branch lengths
Additional sequences increase statistical power, which narrows the credible interval and shifts the point estimate with it
quiz.explanation: The estimate describes the common ancestor of the sequences in hand. Sample one case from an early divergent chain and the tMRCA moves earlier, sometimes substantially — which is why the Bundibugyo team checked stability across four nested datasets.

quiz.question: An ESS of 45 is reported for the clock rate parameter. What follows?
options: The prior is dominating the posterior for that parameter, and it should be widened before the analysis is rerun
The chain has converged adequately, since an effective sample size above 20 indicates sufficient mixing
The credible interval for that parameter is not trustworthy and the chain needs extending
Burn-in was set too high, discarding usable samples from the posterior
quiz.explanation: Effective sample size estimates how many independent draws your correlated MCMC samples are worth. The working convention is above 200 for every reported parameter. Below that the posterior is under-sampled and the interval is unreliable.

quiz.question: How do you test whether the data, rather than the prior, are driving a tMRCA estimate?
options: Increase the chain length until the credible interval stops narrowing
Run the analysis sampling from the prior only and compare the resulting tMRCA
Compare marginal likelihoods between a strict and a relaxed clock model, and take the better-supported one as authoritative
Check that the R-squared of the root-to-tip regression exceeds an agreed threshold before proceeding
quiz.explanation: Sampling from the prior with no data shows you what the model believes before seeing anything. If the tMRCA barely moves when the data are added, the data are not informing it. One extra run, and the single most useful robustness check in phylodynamics.

quiz.question: Which clock model is most defensible for a single-pathogen, single-host outbreak over a 100-day window?
options: A random local clock, which infers where rate shifts occur along the tree
An uncorrelated lognormal relaxed clock, which always accommodates more variation
A strict clock, which is more powerful when a single rate is plausible
A fixed clock rate taken from a previous outbreak of the same pathogen
quiz.explanation: Relaxing costs statistical power and should be justified by a reason for rates to differ — different hosts, chronic versus acute infection, long timescales. None applies here. Fixing the rate from a previous outbreak imports another study's assumption as this study's finding.

exercises.label: Conceptual
exercises.prompt: Write the tMRCA finding from a study as a single sentence for an incident manager. The estimate is 22 February (95% HPDI 16 January – 24 March); the outbreak was declared on 15 May. Then say what three things your sentence deliberately does not claim.
exercises.guidance: ‘The common ancestor of sequenced cases dates to late February 2026 (95% credible interval mid-January to late March), indicating that transmission was established at least six to eight weeks before the outbreak was recognised.’ It does not claim: the date of the index case, the date of spillover, or that this is the age of the outbreak rather than a lower bound conditional on the sequences available.

exercises.label: Read the output
exercises.prompt: A Tracer summary from a BEAST run. Answer the three questions.
questions: One parameter here should stop you quoting the result it governs. Which, and what does it govern?
What is missing from this output that you would need before believing any of the intervals?
The root height HPD spans 0.394 to 0.601 years. Convert that to a plain sentence and note what the asymmetry around the mean tells you.
exercises.guidance: skygrid.precision has an ESS of 96, below the working threshold of 200 — and it is the smoothing parameter of the SkyGrid, so the shape of the Ne curve is under-sampled and should not be quoted as though it were resolved. Missing: evidence of convergence between independent chains. A single converged-looking chain can be stuck in a local optimum, and only this one run is shown. The root height means the common ancestor sits roughly 4.7 to 7.2 months before the most recent sample; the interval is longer on the older side, so the data are more compatible with an older origin than with a younger one — which is the direction that matters, since tMRCA is a lower bound anyway.

exercises.label: Three of six
exercises.prompt: Exactly three of these statements are correct.

statements.text: A tMRCA moves earlier when a sequence from an early divergent chain is added.
Sampling from the prior with no data is a way to test whether the data inform the tMRCA.
An HPD interval is a confidence interval computed from the bootstrap distribution.
A strict clock is more powerful than a relaxed clock when a single rate is plausible.
Longer MCMC chains can create temporal signal that the sampling window does not contain.
The tMRCA is the date the pathogen crossed from its animal reservoir into humans.

exercises.guidance: 1, 2 and 4. An HPD is a direct probability statement about the parameter given model and priors, not a frequentist confidence interval. Chain length improves sampling of the posterior, never the information content of the data. And spillover sits somewhere on the branch leading to the tMRCA node, which may be long.
