lessons.title: Phylodynamics — reading epidemic dynamics off the shape of a tree
lessons.subtitle: And the sensitivity analysis that separates a real slowdown from a sampling slowdown
lessons.description: Coalescent intuition, why effective population size is not prevalence, the four tree priors including SkyGrid, and the nested-truncation analysis that tests whether a curve is real.
lessons.practical: For a published skyline: what are the axis units, what is the grid resolution against the generation time, what did sequencing effort do over the same period, is there a truncation sensitivity analysis, and is the case-based curve on the same figure?

quiz.question: A SkyGrid plot shows effective population size falling in the final four weeks of a dataset. What is the first alternative explanation to test?
options: That sequencing effort declined over the same period
That a fitter lineage has swept, reducing genetic diversity
That the smoothing prior is too strong for the chosen grid resolution
That the clock model has become misspecified toward the present
quiz.explanation: Fewer recent samples means fewer recent coalescences means an apparent fall in Ne. A change in sampling and a change in dynamics look identical, which is why nested-truncation analysis exists. The Bundibugyo team tested exactly this and reported it.

quiz.question: Why is effective population size systematically smaller than the number of infected people?
options: Because overdispersed transmission means a minority of cases cause most transmission
Because Ne counts only infections that were sequenced and passed quality filters
Because generation time is always shorter than the serial interval in practice
Because the coalescent conditions on the sampling process, which removes cases
quiz.explanation: Ne is the size of an idealised population that would produce the observed variability. Real epidemics are overdispersed, and superspreading pushes the effective size well below the census size. Population structure and generation time also separate them, but variance in transmission is the main driver.

quiz.question: SkyGrid with 31 transition points at one-week intervals over a 32-week cutoff means:
options: Ne estimated freely in each weekly block back 32 weeks, with a smoothing prior between blocks
A prior requiring Ne to change by at most one order of magnitude per week
Thirty-one independent MCMC chains, one for each week of the analysis, combined into a single posterior at the end
A requirement that thirty-one sequences be sampled in each of the weekly blocks to give balanced temporal coverage
quiz.explanation: The grid divides the 32 weeks before the most recent sample into weekly blocks, estimating Ne in each with a smoothing prior linking neighbours. Weekly resolution against a two-week serial interval is fine enough to see real change and coarse enough to be estimable.

quiz.question: A doubling time is reported as 21.0 days with a 95% HPDI of 15.0 to 40.7 days. What should the report say?
options: 21 days, since the point estimate is the best available summary
About three weeks, rounding to reflect the imprecision
Between 15 and 41 days, noting the interval is strongly right-skewed
Faster than 21 days, since the interval's lower bound is closer to the point estimate
quiz.explanation: The interval runs to nearly six weeks, so much slower growth is entirely consistent with the data. Reporting the point alone hides that, and the right skew means the usual mental symmetry around a point estimate is wrong here.

quiz.question: Case-based Rt and phylodynamic Re disagree for a given outbreak. What is the correct interpretation?
options: The genomic estimate is authoritative because it captures unobserved transmission
The disagreement is itself the finding, since they have largely independent biases
The case-based estimate is authoritative because it uses more of the data
One of the analyses contains an error that should be found and reconciled
quiz.explanation: They measure related but different things with different blind spots. Agreement is genuine corroboration. Disagreement — classically, flat case counts with rising genomic diversity — usually means transmission continuing outside the surveillance system's view, which is precisely when the genomic result should change the response.

exercises.label: Conceptual
exercises.prompt: A skyline plot shows effective population size rising through May and June then flattening in July. Give three explanations, ranked by how likely you think they are, and say what single extra piece of data would separate them.
exercises.guidance: Most likely: sequencing effort fell in July, so fewer recent coalescences produce an apparent flattening. Next: the epidemic genuinely slowed, from control measures or susceptible depletion. Least likely without other evidence: a change in transmission structure. The separating data is sequences-per-week over the same period, overlaid on the curve — and the formal version is a nested-truncation analysis with identical curation at each cutoff.

exercises.label: Read the output
exercises.prompt: A SkyGrid result table with the sequencing effort alongside it.
questions: Describe what the Ne column alone appears to show, then what the last column does to that reading.
The HPD intervals behave in a specific way over the last four weeks. Describe it and explain the cause.
Can you convert the final Ne·τ of 36.2 into a number of infections? What would you need?
exercises.guidance: The Ne column alone reads as growth to a plateau around late June, i.e. an epidemic being brought under control. The genome column shows sequencing collapsing from 102 to 9 per week over the same period, which is exactly what produces an apparent plateau — fewer recent coalescences. The HPD intervals widen sharply (74 wide, then 62, then 71, then 87) while the median barely moves: the data are running out, so the smoothing prior rather than the data is increasingly determining the curve. And no: Ne·τ is not prevalence. You would need the generation time to divide by, and even then overdispersed transmission and population structure separate effective from census size, usually by a large factor.

exercises.label: Three of six
exercises.prompt: Exactly three of these statements are correct.

statements.text: Coalescence rate is inversely proportional to effective population size.
Superspreading raises effective population size above the census number infected.
Birth-death models estimate Re directly and model sampling explicitly.
A finer SkyGrid resolution always gives a more informative curve.
Doubling time is ln(2) divided by the exponential growth rate.
Agreement between case-based Rt and phylodynamic Re means one of them is redundant.

exercises.guidance: 1, 3 and 5. Overdispersed transmission pushes Ne well below the census size, not above. Too fine a grid leaves each interval with almost no coalescent events, so the smoothing prior rather than the data determines the curve. And agreement between two measurements with largely independent biases is corroboration, which is exactly why both are worth having.

exercises.label: Scaffolded
exercises.prompt: Design the sensitivity analysis. Three of the four steps are given.
exercises.output:

  Step 4  Compare clock rate and tMRCA across them  ✓

  What the result can show: ______________________
  What it cannot show: ______________________
exercises.guidance: Step 2: apply identical curation and filtering to each dataset — without that, differences between the runs are differences in how you treated them. It can show that the conclusion is not an artefact of where you cut the data: in the published case, clock rates converged at ~8.5e-4 across the later datasets and the tMRCA was stable from July onward. It cannot rescue you from bias that ran in the same direction throughout, which is why the authors still flagged possible missing diversity in the two months around and preceding the inferred tMRCA.

lessons.phase_title: From data to trees to time
lessons.title: Where it came from — phylogeography, introductions, and the sampling bias that eats it
lessons.subtitle: Discrete trait analysis will place the origin wherever you sequenced most
lessons.description: Discrete trait analysis and its failure mode, structured coalescent alternatives, what an introduction count depends on, and the same machinery applied to hosts rather than places.
lessons.practical: For a published phylogeographic analysis: compute sequences-per-case by location and check whether the inferred origin is also the best-sampled location. Then rewrite the origin claim as observation, hedged inference, and alternative explanation.

quiz.question: Country A sequenced 5,000 cases; neighbouring Country B sequenced 50. A discrete trait analysis infers the epidemic originated in A. What is the main concern?
options: The clock rate almost certainly differs between the two countries, which biases the ancestral node dates the model reconstructs
The tree prior assumed a single well-mixed population across both countries
The migration rate matrix between the two countries is likely too sparsely populated to be estimated reliably
DTA knows only how many sequences you supplied, not how many infections exist
quiz.explanation: Discrete trait analysis treats location as a trait on a tree whose shape came from a coalescent that knows nothing about location. Most of the tree is in A because most sequences are, so A is inferred as ancestral — regardless of the truth.

quiz.question: What is the principal advantage of a structured coalescent method over discrete trait analysis?
options: It runs substantially faster on datasets with many locations
It separates deme population size from sampling intensity
It does not require sampling dates to be known precisely
It permits continuous rather than discrete location variables
quiz.explanation: The structured coalescent models subpopulations with their own sizes connected by migration, so a deme can be large and barely sampled and the model can represent that. The cost is more parameters, heavier computation and a practical limit on the number of demes.

quiz.question: An introduction count of 'at least 12 independent introductions' is preferred to '12 introductions' because:
options: Introduction counts are conventionally reported as lower bounds in the literature
The Bayesian posterior for a count is always right-skewed
Twelve is within the credible interval rather than at its mode
Introductions from unsampled locations may have been merged or missed
quiz.explanation: The count depends jointly on local sampling fraction, external sampling, the clustering rule and the time window. Denser sampling resolves single introductions into several, and unsampled sources get merged — so the number is a floor, not a measurement.

quiz.question: Applying phylogeographic machinery to hosts rather than places, what does a single monophyletic clade of cattle sequences indicate?
options: Repeated independent spillovers from the same bird lineage
A single cross-species jump followed by onward transmission within cattle
Ongoing bidirectional transmission between cattle and birds
That cattle sequences were all generated in a single laboratory batch
quiz.explanation: One clade means one successful jump; several scattered clades nested among bird sequences would mean several. This is exactly the logic that established a single B3.13 spillover into US dairy cattle — and it is bounded by how well the bird reservoir was sampled.

quiz.question: Why does subsampling not fix a phylogeographic dataset in which one region has zero sequences?
options: No statistical procedure recovers a location that was never sequenced
Subsampling requires equal case counts, not equal sequence counts
Subsampling reduces power, and the remaining sequences would be too few
Zero-count locations violate the Markov assumption of the trait model
quiz.explanation: Subsampling equalises among the locations you have. An empty region simply does not exist to the model, and transmission through it is attributed to the sampled locations either side. This is why sequencing equity is a methodological precondition rather than a fairness supplement.

exercises.label: Conceptual
exercises.prompt: Explain in two sentences, to someone with no phylogenetics, why a phylogeographic analysis can produce a map of laboratory funding rather than a map of the epidemic.
exercises.guidance: The method reconstructs where each ancestor probably was by looking at where its descendants were sampled — but it only knows how many sequences you gave it, not how many infections exist in each place. So a country that sequences a lot appears as the origin and a country that sequences little appears to receive, regardless of what actually happened.

exercises.guidance: Almost none of it is evidence about the epidemic. A supplied 4,812 of 4,933 sequences — 98% of the tree is in A, so A is inferred as ancestral more or less by construction. You would use a structured coalescent, which separates deme size from sampling intensity, or subsample toward case counts and repeat across replicates. What no method can fix is a region with zero sequences — it does not exist to the model, and transmission through it is attributed to whatever was sampled either side.

exercises.guidance: 1, 2 and 4. Subsampling equalises among the locations you have and cannot conjure one you do not. DTA models location as a trait on the tree and knows only sequence counts. And continuous phylogeography inherits exactly the same sampling problem, in continuous form.

lessons.title: Clusters, transmission and the language of genomic evidence
lessons.subtitle: The sentences you are actually entitled to write
lessons.description: The three strengths of genomic statement, how genomic and epidemiological evidence cover each other's blind spots, what transmission-tree software really outputs, and four questions genomics answers well.
topics: Relapse vs reinfection; import vs residual
lessons.practical: Take an outbreak investigation with sequences. For each case pair, place the evidence into one of the three strengths and write the sentence. Then delete every use of 'confirmed' that is not an exclusion.

quiz.question: Two isolates are identical. What is the strongest defensible genomic statement?
options: This is consistent with direct transmission and with several other histories
The two cases belong to the same transmission chain, though direction is unknown
Direct transmission between these two cases is confirmed by the sequence data
One case infected the other, with the direction determined by sampling dates
quiz.explanation: With under one substitution per transmission, identity is consistent with direct transmission, a short unsampled chain, and two infections from a common source. Sampling dates do not establish direction, and the word confirmed belongs only to exclusions.

quiz.question: Which cell of the genomic-versus-epidemiological evidence table is most productive for an investigation?
options: No epidemiological link and genomically compatible
Epidemiological link present and genomically excluded
No epidemiological link and genomically excluded
Epidemiological link present and genomically compatible
quiz.explanation: Compatible genomes with no known contact point at a missing piece of the network — an unrecognised setting, an asymptomatic chain, a shared exposure. In hospital investigations this is the routine finding, and it is what leads to the shared equipment or the environmental reservoir.

quiz.question: What does transmission-tree inference software such as TransPhylo actually output?
options: A network of contacts weighted by genetic distance
The most likely chain of infections, with each link's probability
A ranked list of candidate index cases with posterior support
A posterior distribution over transmission trees accommodating unsampled cases
quiz.explanation: The output is a distribution, and its legitimate uses are estimating unobserved transmission and the offspring distribution. Presenting the maximum a posteriori tree as the transmission tree discards the method's whole contribution — and naming individuals raises ethical problems beyond the statistical ones.

quiz.question: A patient has two TB episodes. Whole genome sequencing shows the isolates are near-identical. What does this indicate?
options: Laboratory cross-contamination between the two specimens
Relapse — the original infection persisted and regrew
Reinfection from a household contact carrying the same circulating strain
A mixed infection in which one strain was below threshold initially
quiz.explanation: Near-identity between two episodes in one patient indicates the original population persisted rather than a new infection arriving. The same design settled the equivalent question in gambiense HAT, where sequencing showed relapse was parasite regrowth rather than reinfection — a statement about drug efficacy, not transmission.

quiz.question: Which element is most often missing from a published cluster definition?
options: The number of isolates assigned to each cluster
The genetic distance threshold applied
The pathogen and the reference genome used
The local background distance distribution among unlinked isolates
quiz.explanation: Thresholds are almost always stated; backgrounds almost never are. Without knowing how far apart unlinked local isolates typically sit, the threshold carries no information about how surprising the cluster is. The linkage rule is the second most commonly omitted element.

exercises.label: Conceptual
exercises.prompt: An incident manager asks: “did case 14 infect case 17?” The two genomes are identical. Give the answer you are entitled to give, and then give the answer they were hoping for and explain why you cannot give it.
exercises.guidance: Entitled: the isolates are identical, which is consistent with direct transmission and equally consistent with a short chain through unsampled cases or with two infections from a common source. Hoped for: yes. You cannot give it because at well under one substitution per transmission, identity carries almost no discriminating power — and sequence data does not give direction even when a link is real.

exercises.label: Read the output
exercises.prompt: A pairwise SNP matrix from a suspected ward outbreak, with the epidemiological summary beneath it.
exercises.output:
P01   P02   P03   P04   P05
  P01       —     0     1    31     2
  P02       0     —     1    29     2
  P03       1     1     —    30     1
  P04      31    29    30     —    28
  P05       2     2     1    28     —

  Background: pairwise distance among contemporaneous unlinked isolates
              in this hospital, median 24 SNPs (IQR 17–33)

  Ward overlap:  P01–P02 yes   P01–P03 yes   P04 yes (same ward, same week)
                 P05 NO — never admitted to this ward
questions: Which patient can you exclude from the cluster, and how confident is that statement compared with the others you could make?
P05 has no ward contact but sits within 2 SNPs of the cluster. Which cell of the evidence table is this, and what should happen next?
Write the cluster definition sentence you would put in the report.
exercises.guidance: P04 is excluded: 28–31 SNPs, squarely inside the unlinked background distribution, is inconsistent with recent transmission. That is the strongest statement available here — exclusion is robust to incomplete sampling, because unsampled intermediates would make distances larger, not smaller. P05 is the productive cell: genomically compatible with no known epidemiological link, which points at a missing part of the network — shared staff, shared equipment, an environmental reservoir, or an unrecognised contact. That is what to investigate, not a reason to dismiss the genomics. Report sentence: ‘P01, P02, P03 and P05 fall within 2 SNPs of one another against a local background of 24 SNPs (IQR 17–33) among contemporaneous unlinked isolates, sampled within a 3-week window; P04 differs by 28–31 SNPs and a direct link to this cluster is excluded.’

exercises.label: Three of six
exercises.prompt: Exactly three of these statements are correct.

statements.text: Exclusion is robust to incomplete sampling because unsampled intermediates would increase, not decrease, genetic distance.
Transmission-tree software returns a posterior distribution over transmission trees.
Near-identical isolates from two episodes in one patient indicate reinfection.
Distinguishing importation from residual transmission requires a historical sequence archive from that focus.
The word 'confirmed' is appropriate for a genomic linkage finding supported by identical genomes.
A survivor-associated flare-up typically attaches to a recent part of the tree on a short branch.

exercises.guidance: 1, 2 and 4. Near-identity between two episodes in one patient indicates relapse — the original population persisted — which is how the question was settled in gambiense HAT and is used routinely in TB and malaria. ‘Confirmed’ belongs to exclusions only. And a survivor-associated flare-up shows the opposite signature: a long branch attaching to an old part of the tree, sometimes with an unusually low apparent rate.

exercises.label: Scaffolded
exercises.prompt: Convert each finding into the sentence you are entitled to write. The strength is given; supply the sentence.
exercises.output:
Finding                                      Strength        Sentence
  ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  27 SNPs apart, rate ~16/genome/yr            exclusion       ____________
  identical, documented shared exposure        consistency     ____________
  identical, no known contact                  consistency     ____________
  71% coverage, differences in dropout region  indeterminacy   ____________
exercises.guidance: Exclusion: ‘...this is inconsistent with direct transmission during the outbreak period; a direct link is excluded.’ Consistency with epi: ‘...in isolation this is consistent with direct transmission and with transmission through unsampled intermediates; together with the documented shared exposure the combined evidence supports a link, though direction cannot be determined from sequence data.’ Consistency without epi: ‘...consistent with a chain passing through unsampled cases; warrants targeted investigation; does not establish direct links between the sampled cases.’ Indeterminacy: ‘...this sample cannot be placed relative to the cluster at the required resolution.’

exercises.prompt: Take an outbreak investigation with sequences. For each case pair, place the evidence into one of the three strengths and write the sentence. Then delete every use of 'confirmed' that is not an exclusion.
exercises.guidance: No single right answer. The value is in doing it on data you actually have, where you know what the numbers mean and can tell when an answer is implausible.

lessons.title: Sampling and metadata — the two things that decide whether any of it is true
lessons.subtitle: A modest sequencer with a defensible frame beats a NovaSeq with convenience sampling
lessons.description: Four sampling strategies for four objectives, the 3/p rule for detecting a variant, the minimum metadata set, and how to evaluate a genomic surveillance system.
lessons.practical: For a system you know: name its objective, compute sequences-per-case across strata, compute metadata completeness for the ten core fields, compute median and 90th-percentile turnaround, and list the decisions it changed in twelve months.

quiz.question: A national dataset mixes routine sentinel sequences, outbreak investigation sequences and traveller screening sequences, then reports national lineage proportions. What is wrong?
options: Outbreak investigation sequences are over-represented relative to their share of the national case count for the period
The sequences were generated on different sequencing platforms with different error profiles and are not comparable
Three different selection processes are being analysed as though they were one
Traveller sequences should be excluded because importations are not local transmission
quiz.explanation: Each frame samples a different population. Pooled, the national picture is a composite, and apparent trends can be produced entirely by shifts in the mix. This is why sampling frame belongs as a field on every sequence — the highest-value metadata item almost nobody collects.

quiz.question: Approximately how many sequences are needed for 95% confidence of detecting at least one case of a variant circulating at 1%, under simple random sampling?
options: About 30
About 1,000
About 100
About 300
quiz.explanation: n = ln(0.05)/ln(1-p), which is approximately 3/p — so about 299. The real requirement is larger once case ascertainment, geographic clustering and the sequencing cascade are accounted for, since none of those is simple random sampling.

quiz.question: A programme records the date a sample arrived at the laboratory instead of the date it was collected. What is the epidemiological consequence?
options: Remote areas appear later because transport delay is longer, creating spurious spread patterns
A uniform shift in all node dates that cancels out in relative comparisons
Loss of temporal signal, making the dataset undatable
Overestimation of the evolutionary rate proportional to the mean delay
quiz.explanation: The delay is not uniform — it is longer for remote areas. Those health zones' tips shift later relative to central ones, which feeds phylogeographic inference and manufactures a centre-to-periphery spread pattern. A clerical shortcut becomes a published conclusion.

quiz.question: Which is the strongest argument that adding a metadata field can be worth more than adding a sequencer?
options: Metadata fields cost nothing to collect once a system is in place
Without case linkage, no number of genomes can answer severity or outcome questions
Sequencing instruments depreciate over a five-year cycle whereas a metadata schema, once designed, retains its value indefinitely
Regulatory frameworks require metadata but do not mandate sequencing volume
quiz.explanation: A programme sequencing 100 genomes a month with complete case linkage can answer severity, outcome and vaccine-effectiveness questions. A programme sequencing 1,000 with laboratory data alone can answer none of them, at any volume.

quiz.question: What should sit at the top of a genomic surveillance system's evaluation metrics?
options: Percentage of genomes exceeding the completeness threshold
Median turnaround time from collection to database deposition
Decisions changed, logged with date and counterfactual
Genomes produced per month, as the primary output measure
quiz.explanation: The other three are inputs. A programme that cannot name decisions it changed is producing data rather than surveillance, and the decisions log is also its best protection when it is asked to justify its budget.

exercises.label: Conceptual
exercises.prompt: A programme sequences 300 samples a month and states it can detect a variant at 1% prevalence. Say why that is wrong in a knowable direction, and write the defensible version.
exercises.guidance: n ≈ 3/p gives ~300 for 1% — but only under simple random sampling from all infections. You sample from detected cases, so ascertainment enters; a new variant emerges locally rather than uniformly; and the Ct gate plus the coverage threshold remove low-load samples non-randomly. The defensible version states the assumed ascertainment fraction and sequencing success rate and reports detectable prevalence as a range rather than a point.

exercises.label: Read the output
exercises.prompt: A surveillance system evaluation table. Answer the three questions.
questions: The national metadata figures look tolerable. What do the strata show that the national row hides?
Which single metadata column would most increase what this system can answer, and what class of question does it unlock?
Interpret the turnaround distribution against a decision requiring an answer within two weeks.
exercises.guidance: The national row is dominated by the capital, which supplied 83% of sequences but 26% of cases. Everything degrades with distance from the capital, and the degradation is correlated across columns — the places with the fewest sequences also have the worst dates and no case linkage at all. Case ID link is the column to fix: it unlocks every clinical question — severity, outcome, vaccine effectiveness — none of which any number of genomes can answer without it. On turnaround: a 9-day median meets a two-week requirement, but the 90th percentile of 48 days does not, and the late tail will be the remote provinces, which are exactly where undetected transmission is most likely. Report the distribution, never the mean.

exercises.label: Three of six
exercises.prompt: Exactly three of these statements are correct.

statements.text: Targeted risk-based sampling is efficient for detection and unusable for estimating proportions.
Recording the sampling frame on each sequence is among the highest-value metadata additions.
Substituting the laboratory receipt date for the collection date shifts all tips equally and cancels out.
Detecting a variant at 0.1% prevalence needs roughly 3,000 sequences under random sampling.
A system's representativeness is best summarised by the total number of genomes produced.
Sentinel sampling supports valid national lineage proportion estimates.

exercises.guidance: 1, 2 and 4. The receipt-date shift is longer for remote areas, so it makes them appear systematically later and manufactures a centre-to-periphery spread pattern. Representativeness is sequences per case by stratum — the ratio, not the count. And sentinel sampling represents its catchments, so it is good for detecting change over time and poor for national proportions.

exercises.label: Scaffolded
exercises.prompt: Match each objective to its frame and to the metadata field that most constrains it. Two rows are done.
exercises.output:
objective                          frame                 constraining field
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
national lineage proportions       representative random  sampling frame  ✓
detect a new variant early         targeted + sentinel    ______________
outbreak reconstruction            ______________         ______________
severity of a lineage              ______________         outcome, vaccination  ✓
reservoir / One Health             ______________         ______________
exercises.guidance: Detect early: date and location, plus the clinical or diagnostic anomaly that triggered selection. Outbreak reconstruction: universal within the outbreak, constrained by collection date at real precision plus the case ID link. Severity: representative sampling plus case linkage — the frame matters as much as the outcome field, because a targeted set inflates severity. Reservoir: targeted across hosts, constrained by host species and geography, and the deciding issue is comparable intensity across hosts rather than absolute numbers.

lessons.title: Sharing, governance and equity — where the sequence goes, and who decides
lessons.subtitle: Unsequenced regions do not leave gaps, they cause wrong answers
lessons.description: INSDC, GISAID and Pathoplexus compared, why immediate open sharing is not simply right, Nagoya/DSI and the PABS negotiations, human read depletion, and equity as a methodological requirement.
topics: Nagoya, DSI, the Cali Fund, PABS
lessons.practical: For a dataset your institution holds: where is it deposited, what terms apply and who decided, are human reads depleted and verified, could an individual be re-identified, and what is your institution's position if someone else publishes it tomorrow?

quiz.question: Why are the 2026 Bundibugyo genomes deposited under a restricted licence with named contacts?
options: Because national law in the DRC prohibits the open deposition of pathogen sequence data derived from human samples
Because Pathoplexus does not support fully open deposition for risk group 4 pathogens
Because filovirus sequences are considered dual-use research of concern and are therefore subject to biosecurity export controls
So the institution that generated them retains control until it publishes its own analysis
quiz.explanation: The restricted period addresses the helicopter-research problem: a team doing the fieldwork can be scooped by better-resourced analysts. The analysis itself was posted publicly during the outbreak — the design delivers most of both openness and equity.

quiz.question: What is the principal scientific cost of GISAID's model relative to INSDC?
options: Redistribution is prohibited, making reproducible analyses harder to build
Metadata fields are fewer, limiting phylogeographic inference
Sequence quality is not validated before deposition
Sequences are deposited later, because the terms of use must be accepted before submission is possible
quiz.explanation: The prohibition on redistribution means pipelines must handle access control and published analyses cannot ship their input data. That is a real reproducibility cost — set against the achievement of getting sequences shared at speed from countries that would not have used a fully open database.

quiz.question: What is the status of the WHO Pandemic Agreement's PABS annex as of mid-2026?
options: Still under negotiation, with a final outcome due at the Assembly in May 2027
Adopted at the World Health Assembly in May 2026 and now in force
Merged into the Convention on Biological Diversity's digital sequence information mechanism agreed at COP16
Abandoned after negotiations failed in early 2026, with a network of bilateral agreements now replacing the multilateral approach
quiz.explanation: Member States extended negotiations through 2026 and decided in May 2026 that a final negotiated outcome would be presented for adoption in May 2027. The unresolved core is mandatory benefit sharing as the condition for rapid pathogen information sharing.

quiz.question: Why is human read depletion before deposition a legal requirement and not only good practice?
options: Host sequence interferes with automated lineage assignment
Sequence repositories automatically reject any submission found to contain off-target host reads
Human genomic data is identifiable and regulated as personal data
Host reads inflate file sizes beyond repository submission limits
quiz.explanation: Any clinical sample carries host nucleic acid, and metagenomic data is mostly human. Identifiable human genetic data is regulated in the EU and many other jurisdictions, and the depletion step falls in the gap between the bioinformatician and the data protection officer.

quiz.question: In what order does this course expect the binding constraints on genomic surveillance capacity to fall?
options: Metadata linkage, then analysts, then compute, then sequencers
Compute, then sequencers, then metadata linkage, then analysts
Sequencers, then compute, then analysts, then metadata linkage
Analysts, then sequencers, then metadata linkage, then compute
quiz.explanation: Instruments are purchasable, analysts are trainable but slowly, and linking sequences to case records requires organisational change no grant buys. Most funding is allocated in the reverse order, which is why sequencing capacity has expanded faster than the ability to use it.

exercises.label: Conceptual
exercises.prompt: Give the strongest argument you can for immediate open deposition, then the strongest against, then say what the 2026 Bundibugyo team actually did and why it gets most of both.
exercises.guidance: For: unsequenced or unshared regions do not merely leave gaps — they make phylogeographic inference actively wrong for everyone, so withholding degrades the science globally. Against: a researcher who does the fieldwork can be scooped by better-resourced analysts, local analytical capacity never develops, and sequences derive from human samples under national law and specific consent. What they did: posted the full analysis publicly on virological.org during the outbreak, while depositing the sequences under a restricted licence with named institutional contacts. The world could see the methods, the trees and the numbers in real time; control of the data stayed with the institution that generated it.

exercises.label: Read the output
exercises.prompt: A database record for an outbreak dataset. Answer the three questions.
exercises.output:
Platform         Pathoplexus
Dataset          BDBV_DRC_20260820   (PP_SS_3400.1)
Sequences        525
Licence          RESTRICTED — contact required prior to use in advance of publication
Contacts         Dr T. Wawina-Bokalanga; Prof. P. Mbala-Kingebeni (INRB, Kinshasa)
Metadata fields  collection_date, health_zone, host, specimen_type, ct_value
Host reads       depleted (verified)
Redistribution   permitted after restriction lifts
questions: Compare this record's redistribution term with GISAID's, and say what each choice costs.
'Host reads depleted (verified)' is a technical line with a legal meaning. What is it?
Two metadata fields here are unusual and useful. Which, and what do they let a reader do?
exercises.guidance: Pathoplexus permits redistribution once the restriction lifts, so reproducible analyses can eventually ship their input data; GISAID prohibits it permanently, which is a real reproducibility cost paid in exchange for having got data shared at speed from countries that would not have used a fully open database. Host read depletion matters because clinical samples contain human nucleic acid, which is identifiable and regulated as personal data — depositing without depletion is a data-protection incident, and the step falls in the gap between the bioinformatician and the data protection officer. The unusual fields are specimen_type and ct_value: specimen type reveals that oral fluid from deceased patients is in the dataset, and Ct lets a reader reconstruct the load-based selection rather than take the sampling frame on trust.

exercises.label: Three of six
exercises.prompt: Exactly three of these statements are correct.

statements.text: The Cali Fund is a multilateral mechanism for benefit sharing from use of digital sequence information.
The WHO Pandemic Agreement's PABS annex was adopted in May 2026 and is in force.
Public research and academic institutions are not expected to make monetary contributions to the Cali Fund.
Sequencing equity is an ethical consideration layered on top of otherwise sound methods.
Africa CDC's Africa PGI expanded sequencing capacity from 7 African Union member states in 2019 to 46 by late 2025.
Rich metadata reduces re-identification risk by diluting any single identifying field.

exercises.guidance: 1, 3 and 5. PABS negotiations were extended through 2026 with a final outcome due at the World Health Assembly in May 2027. Equity is a precondition for correct inference, not a supplement to it — empty regions make the model wrong, not merely incomplete. And rich metadata increases re-identification risk: in a small health zone, sex, age, village and onset date together are identifying.

exercises.label: Scaffolded
exercises.prompt: A submission checklist with three items completed. Fill the rest, then answer the last line.
exercises.output:

  2. Metadata deposited ...... collection_date, location, host, specimen  ✓
  3. Human reads ............. depleted and verified  ✓
  4. Terms stated ............ ______________

exercises.guidance: Platform: for outbreak sequences you need to control while your own team analyses them, Pathoplexus with a restricted period; for routine or retrospective work, INSDC. Terms: state the restriction, state until when, and name a contact. Analysis: publish it even while sequences are restricted — virological.org, a preprint, a Nextstrain build, a national bulletin. The last line is the one to answer before it happens rather than after; an institution that has not decided will decide badly and under pressure.

lessons.title: From genome to decision — what genomic surveillance is actually for
lessons.subtitle: A programme that cannot name the decisions it changed is producing data, not surveillance
lessons.description: The decisions genomics changes, the four-question 'so what' test, deriving timeliness from the decision, writing for an incident management team, and when genomics is the wrong tool.
topics: When genomics is the wrong tool
lessons.practical: Capstone: design a genomic surveillance activity on one page — decision, question, sampling frame, the arithmetic, platform, metadata, timeliness, analysis, sharing, the result that would change the decision, and the limitation you already know you will write.

quiz.question: Which question does this course say most genomic surveillance activities fail?
options: What confidence is needed, and does the sampling support it
What result would change the decision, and in which direction
By when must the answer arrive
What decision could this change, and who makes it
quiz.explanation: Most activities can gesture at a decision; almost none pre-specify the result that would change it. Deciding the threshold before seeing the data is what separates surveillance from interpretation after the fact — and failing the decision question at all means the activity is research, which should be funded as research.

quiz.question: Why should turnaround time be reported as a distribution rather than a mean?
options: Turnaround times are log-normally distributed, so the mean is undefined
Regulatory reporting standards require percentiles rather than averages
Means are sensitive to the batch size chosen for each sequencing run
A long tail affects the remote samples where the interesting cases are
quiz.explanation: A median of 6 days with a 90th percentile of 40 days is a system that works on average and fails exactly where samples travel furthest — which is where undetected transmission is most likely. The mean conceals precisely the failure that matters.

quiz.question: A genomic finding for an incident management team should always include which element that papers routinely omit?
options: The substitution model and support values used
The credible interval attached to every quantitative estimate presented
An explicit statement of what was not sequenced
The database accession numbers for the sequences
quiz.explanation: One clause naming the cases that were not sequenced is the single most important limitation and the easiest to leave out. Model details belong in the methods, not in an operational brief, and credible intervals are usually better expressed as calibrated confidence words for this audience.

quiz.question: Which is a legitimate reason to conclude that sequencing is the wrong tool for a question?
options: The laboratory has no experience with the relevant amplicon scheme
Sequences from neighbouring countries are not available for context
The results would take three weeks and the outbreak is expected to last three months
The pathogen accumulates too few substitutions per transmission to resolve the question
quiz.explanation: Lesson 1's arithmetic can rule a question out before any money is spent. The other three are operational obstacles that can be addressed; an inadequate clock cannot be fixed by more sequencing, more depth or a better platform.

quiz.question: The course argues the opportunity cost of a sequencer is often what?
options: Cold chain and connectivity infrastructure at peripheral collection sites, without which samples never arrive
A second sequencer of a different platform for cross-validation
A data manager, who frequently buys more epidemiology per euro
Reagent stock sufficient to keep the instrument saturated
quiz.explanation: In a programme where a large fraction of cases have no recorded onset date, fixing the metadata buys more usable epidemiology than sequencing more samples. This is the practical form of the course's spine: sampling and metadata, not the sequencer.

exercises.label: Conceptual
exercises.prompt: Name three genomic surveillance activities you have seen proposed or funded that would fail question 1 of the so-what test, and say what should have happened to each.
exercises.guidance: The pattern to look for is any activity whose stated purpose is ‘improve understanding’, ‘build capacity’ or ‘characterise circulating diversity’ with no named decision and no named decision-maker. None of those is illegitimate — they are research, or infrastructure — and each should have been funded, staffed and evaluated as such, with research outputs rather than surveillance metrics.

exercises.label: Read the output
exercises.prompt: An annual report from a genomic surveillance programme. Answer the three questions.
exercises.output:
GENOMIC SURVEILLANCE PROGRAMME — ANNUAL SUMMARY

  Genomes sequenced ................ 8,412   (↑31% on previous year)
  Median turnaround ................ 6 days
  Sequences deposited .............. 8,201 (97.5%)
  Publications ..................... 4 peer-reviewed, 11 preprints
  Staff trained .................... 26
  Cost per genome .................. €41  (↓18%)

  Decisions changed ................ not recorded
questions: Every metric here is an input except one absence. Rewrite the top line of this report as it should read.
Cost per genome fell 18% and is presented as a success. Under what circumstance is that a failure?
The programme is asked to justify its budget in a contracting fiscal year. Which single artefact, started a year ago, would have protected it?
exercises.guidance: The top line should be decisions changed, logged with date, the genomic finding, and what would have happened otherwise. Everything above it is throughput. Falling cost per genome is a failure when it was achieved by sequencing more of the easy samples — high-load, capital-city, already-well-covered — because that improves the denominator while making representativeness worse; the honest denominator is cost per decision-relevant result, which is a much larger and much more useful number. The protective artefact is the decisions log: it is a small ongoing task and it is the only thing that answers the budget question in the programme's own terms.

exercises.label: Three of six
exercises.prompt: Exactly three of these statements are correct.

statements.text: Timeliness requirements should be derived backwards from the decision, not asserted generally.
A finding for an incident manager should always state what was not sequenced.
A mature programme rarely has to say that sequencing cannot answer a question.
Cost per genome is the appropriate denominator for judging programme value.
'No lineage dominance and no fitness-altering mutations' is a result that justifies continuing the current response.
If a result would arrive after the decision point, it retains most of its value as a retrospective record.

exercises.guidance: 1, 2 and 5. A mature programme declines questions regularly; one that always finds something is over-interpreting. Cost per genome rewards volume. And a result arriving after the decision has zero value for that decision and non-zero cost — retrospective value is a different and much weaker claim that should be argued, not assumed.

exercises.prompt: Turn a finding into an incident-management brief. The finding is given; write the four sentences.

Note that the confidence word is calibrated and the reason for it is given in the same sentence.

lessons.title: Bundibugyo virus in Ituri, DRC, 2026 — a 100-day window, line by line
lessons.subtitle: Every methodological choice in the flagship study, including the ones the authors assumed you knew
lessons.description: The 2026 BDBV outbreak analysis decoded phrase by phrase: amplicon-nf, the ADAR exclusion, GTR+F+R3, residual-minimising rooting, BEAST X, SkyGrid, and the nested-truncation sensitivity analysis that makes it trustworthy.
topics: The outbreak and the four questions
The negative finding on lineage dominance
lessons.practical: Read the virological.org post alongside this deep dive. Then list every methodological phrase in it and check you can say which lesson covers it and what it would cost to get wrong.

quiz.question: Why did the Bundibugyo team exclude 32 genomes showing an excess of T-to-C changes?
options: They were duplicate submissions taken from the same patients at different timepoints during their admission
They fell below the genome completeness threshold used for the analysis
They originated from the single Nord-Kivu health zone and were geographically unrepresentative
ADAR host editing is not viral evolution, and it biases the clock the analysis depends on
quiz.explanation: ADAR-edited sites are host-imposed damage, not the virus's replication history. Left in, they inflate the substitution rate, create spurious long branches that distort the coalescent growth estimates, and appear homoplastically across unrelated tips. The clock is the parameter the filter protects.

quiz.question: The analysis reports a root-to-tip regression slope of 7.9e-4 and a Bayesian clock rate of 8.5e-4. Why report both?
options: The two apply to different subsets: 626 genomes and 525 genomes respectively
Agreement between a quick heuristic and a full model is genuine cross-validation
Regression estimates the mutation rate while the Bayesian model estimates the substitution rate
The regression provides the prior from which the Bayesian estimate is drawn
quiz.explanation: The regression is a diagnostic, not an estimator — its tips are non-independent and it understates uncertainty. Its value is as an independent sanity check on the expensive model. A heuristic validating itself would be circular; two methods agreeing is reassurance.

quiz.question: What did the iterative cutoff analysis with datasets ending 23 June, 3 July, 16 July and 9 August establish?
options: That the outbreak was declining, since later datasets showed lower growth rates
That the conclusions were not an artefact of curation or of where the data were cut
That sequencing coverage was adequate in every health zone across the period
That the substitution model chosen by ModelFinder remained stable as further sequences accumulated in each successive dataset
quiz.explanation: Clock rates converged to about 8.5e-4 across later datasets and the tMRCA was stable from July onward. That earns the claim that recent inferences reflect real dynamics rather than the reduced sampling after mid-July — but it cannot rescue bias that ran throughout in one direction, and the authors say so.

quiz.question: Why is 'no fitness-altering mutations and no lineage dominance' described as one of the study's most operationally useful findings?
options: With no licensed countermeasure, the response depends entirely on diagnostics and tracing
It permits the phylogeny to be built under a strict rather than relaxed clock
It establishes that the outbreak originated from a single spillover event
It confirms that the sequencing pipeline used across the outbreak was free of systematic error
quiz.explanation: There is no licensed vaccine or therapeutic for Bundibugyo virus, so the entire response rests on diagnostics, isolation and contact tracing. A negative finding on viral change is what tells the response those assumptions still hold — and it costs as much work as a positive one.

quiz.question: Which weakness of the post does this deep dive identify as most important to look for in the published version?
options: The absence of ESS and chain convergence diagnostics
The use of a 32-week rather than a 52-week SkyGrid cutoff
The decision to trim the alignment to 18,900 bases
The choice of MAFFT rather than a more recent aligner
quiz.explanation: Without ESS above 200 per reported parameter and evidence that independent chains converged, the credible intervals are not trustworthy. The omission is understandable in a work-in-progress post and required in a paper. The other three choices are all defended in the post itself.

quiz.question: What is the reported tMRCA relative to the outbreak's recognition, and how should it be stated?
options: Around 22 February 2026 — at least six to eight weeks before recognition, for sequenced cases
Around 24 April 2026, coinciding exactly with the index case that was identified in Bunia
Around 15 May 2026, the date the outbreak was formally declared
Around 16 January 2026, the earliest bound of the credible interval
quiz.explanation: The point estimate is 22 February with a 95% HPDI from 16 January to 24 March. The correct sentence uses the interval, says 'at least', and says 'of sequenced cases' — because tMRCA is a lower bound on the outbreak's age conditional on the sequences available.

exercises.label: Conceptual
exercises.prompt: The Bundibugyo analysis reports a negative finding — no fitness-altering mutations, no lineage dominance. Explain to a response coordinator why that took as much work as a positive finding, and what it licenses them to do.
exercises.guidance: Establishing that nothing changed requires the same curation, the same clock, the same tree and the same diversity analysis as establishing that something did — plus the sensitivity analysis to show the result is not an artefact of curation or sampling. It licenses the response to keep doing what it is doing: with no licensed vaccine or therapeutic for this species, the response rests entirely on diagnostics, isolation and contact tracing, and this is the finding that says those three assumptions still hold.

exercises.label: Read the output
exercises.prompt: The nested-truncation sensitivity analysis, as a table.
questions: Describe what happens to the clock rate across the four datasets and give the reason.
The HPD width grows as more data are added. Is that the wrong way round?
What does this table license the authors to say, and what does it not license?
exercises.guidance: The clock rate falls from 1.10e-3 and converges on ~8.5e-4. A short sampling window over-estimates the rate, because the temporal signal is thin and the estimate is dominated by whatever divergence happens to be in the earliest and latest tips; adding weeks of range stabilises it. The widening HPD is not wrong: as the tMRCA is pushed earlier, it moves further from the data, and a longer extrapolation carries more uncertainty — the point estimate stabilising while the interval honestly widens is exactly what you want to see. It licenses the claim that the recent inferences are not an artefact of where the data were cut. It does not license any claim about bias that ran in the same direction throughout, which is why the authors separately flag possible missing diversity in the first two months of 2026.

exercises.label: Three of six
exercises.prompt: Exactly three of these statements are correct.

statements.text: The 32 excluded genomes were removed for a mechanistic reason, before the statistical outlier filter ran.
The root-to-tip slope of 7.9e-4 was used as the prior for the Bayesian clock estimate.
525 of 3,748 reported cases were analysed, and reported cases are themselves a fraction of infections.
Bundibugyo virus is a variant of Zaire ebolavirus, so ERVEBO offers partial protection.
SkyGrid's 31 transition points at weekly intervals were chosen to match the serial interval scale.
The post reports ESS values and chain convergence diagnostics.

exercises.guidance: 1, 3 and 5. The root-to-tip slope was an independent cross-check, not a prior — a heuristic validating itself would be circular. Bundibugyo virus is a distinct SPECIES, which is precisely why there is no licensed vaccine or specific therapeutic for it. And ESS and convergence are not reported, which is understandable in a work-in-progress post and is the first thing to look for in the published version.

Collapsed branches → L7; get it wrong and you draw a fully resolved tree from branches resting on no evidence, then argue from its fine structure. SkyGrid → L10; too coarse and you smooth away the feature, too fine and the smoothing prior rather than the data draws the curve. Pathoplexus → L14; get it wrong and you either lose control of your own outbreak data or withhold it in a way that degrades everyone's phylogeography.

lessons.title: Mpox clade Ib — when the host's own enzyme becomes the clock
lessons.subtitle: The same class of process that Deep Dive 1 filters out, used here as the only available signal
lessons.description: How APOBEC3 editing turns a too-slow DNA virus into a datable one, why the same signature is a direct test of sustained human transmission, and the three fragilities of an editing-driven clock.
topics: Why mpox has no usable viral clock
APOBEC3 as clock and as signature
Clade Ib: low diversity, deletions, introductions
lessons.practical: Compare the APOBEC3 and ADAR tables in this deep dive and Lesson 2. Then state the general rule for deciding whether a host editing process is your clock or your artefact.

quiz.question: Why is APOBEC3 editing treated as a clock in mpox but ADAR editing treated as an artefact in filoviruses?
options: APOBEC3 acts on DNA and ADAR on RNA, and only DNA edits are heritable
APOBEC3 edits are randomly distributed whereas ADAR edits cluster in spans
Mpox has no adequate viral clock of its own, whereas filoviruses do
ADAR editing occurs post-mortem in specimens whereas APOBEC3 occurs in living hosts
quiz.explanation: Orthopoxviruses accumulate roughly 0.2 substitutions per genome per year — unusable. Filoviruses manage around 16, which is adequate. When the pathogen's own clock is adequate the editing is noise; when it is not, the editing may be your only signal.

quiz.question: What makes APOBEC3 signature content a direct test of sustained human-to-human transmission?
options: The signature accumulates with human passage, so its abundance indexes human transmission
APOBEC3 is expressed only in humans and not in the animal reservoir species
APOBEC3 mutations are always non-synonymous and therefore visible to selection
The enzyme is induced only during symptomatic infection, marking clinical cases
quiz.explanation: A genome laden with APOBEC3-type changes has passed through humans repeatedly; one without has not. That answers the sustained-transmission-versus-repeated-spillover question from sequence alone, without contact data — though it speaks to the lineage's cumulative history, not to how this particular case was infected.

quiz.question: What is the main methodological fragility of an APOBEC3-driven clock?
options: APOBEC3 mutations revert at a high rate, erasing the signal over time
The mutations are context-dependent and bursty, violating standard substitution models
The signature cannot be distinguished from sequencing error at low coverage
The enzyme edits only the terminal regions of the genome, which are usually trimmed
quiz.explanation: Every standard model assumes substitutions are independent draws from a common process. APOBEC3 mutations are concentrated in TC context, occur in bursts and depend on strand exposure. Fitting a conventional model works well enough to be useful and is a known, open problem.

quiz.question: Clade Ib shows low overall genetic diversity plus a shared large deletion. What does that combination indicate?
options: A single successful introduction into human networks followed by expansion
A slowly evolving virus sampled over a short window
Repeated independent introductions from a common animal source
Extensive recombination between co-circulating lineages homogenising the population
quiz.explanation: Low diversity with a shared structural marker is the signature of recent common ancestry and rapid expansion from one introduction. Distinguishing this from 'slowly evolving virus' requires the clock — which is what APOBEC3 supplies.

exercises.label: Conceptual
exercises.prompt: State the general rule for deciding whether a host editing process is your clock or your artefact, then apply it to a hypothetical: a virus with a viral substitution rate of 4 substitutions per genome per year showing a clear APOBEC3 signature.
exercises.guidance: Ask first whether the pathogen's own clock is adequate for the question. If it is, the editing is noise and you filter it; if it is not, the editing may be your only signal and you must model it, or at minimum say out loud that you did not. At 4 substitutions per genome per year and, say, a two-week serial interval, that is ~0.15 per transmission — marginal. You would probably filter for the tree and report the editing separately as evidence of host passage, rather than letting it drive the clock.

exercises.label: Read the output
exercises.prompt: Mutation spectra for four mpox genomes relative to a clade I reference.
questions: What does the C>T(TC context) column let you say about MPX-101, 102 and 104 that no epidemiological data was needed for?
MPX-103 has three substitutions total. Give the two competing interpretations.
The 1,142 bp deletion is shared by three of the four. What kind of marker is that, and why is it more informative here than most individual substitutions?
exercises.guidance: The APOBEC3 signature is a direct sequence-only test of human passage: a genome carrying many TC-context C>T changes has been transmitting person to person rather than sitting in an animal reservoir. That answered the question that mattered in eastern DRC without contact data. MPX-103 is either a recent zoonotic introduction that has passed through few or no humans, or a sequencing or sampling artefact — check coverage and controls before concluding the former. The deletion is a structural lineage marker, and in a large genome with a very low point-mutation rate a shared structural variant carries more phylogenetic information than most individual substitutions do.

exercises.label: Three of six
exercises.prompt: Exactly three of these statements are correct.

statements.text: APOBEC3 deaminates cytosine in single-stranded DNA, producing C>T changes enriched in TC context.
An APOBEC3-driven clock rate is a property of the virus and transfers between transmission networks.
Standard substitution models assume independence that APOBEC3 mutations violate.
Clade Ib's low genetic diversity indicates a slowly evolving virus rather than a recent expansion.
High APOBEC3 content shows the lineage has passed through humans, not how this case was infected.
Orthopoxvirus baseline substitution rates are adequate for outbreak-scale epidemiology.

exercises.guidance: 1, 3 and 5. The rate reflects host APOBEC3 exposure, which may differ by transmission route, tissue and individual. Low diversity plus a shared deletion is the signature of recent common ancestry and rapid expansion from a single introduction — and distinguishing that from ‘slowly evolving’ is exactly what the clock is needed for. Baseline orthopoxvirus rates are ~0.2 substitutions per genome per year, which is unusable.

exercises.label: Scaffolded
exercises.prompt: Complete the comparison table, then write the one-sentence rule it encodes.

  viral clock without   ~0.2 subs/genome/yr   ______________

Filovirus viral clock: ~16 substitutions per genome per year, which is adequate. Therefore: use APOBEC3 as the clock and as a test of human passage; remove ADAR as an artefact before estimating anything. Rule: the same class of host biology is signal or noise depending entirely on whether the pathogen has an adequate clock of its own.

lessons.title: H5N1 in dairy cattle — one spillover, then two, and what a genotype name carries
lessons.subtitle: A phylogenetic reconstruction describes the past; it does not bound the future
lessons.description: Host-state reconstruction establishing a single B3.13 spillover into US dairy cattle, why only a genotype name could carry the finding, polymerase adaptation as a hypothesis about phenotype, and the independent D1.1 introduction that followed.
topics: Adaptation markers PB2 M631L, PA K497R
lessons.practical: Apply the one-clade-versus-many-clades logic to a reservoir question in your own field. What sampling of the source population would you need before the conclusion is safe?

quiz.question: Cattle H5N1 sequences form a single monophyletic clade descending from a bird-derived ancestor. What does this establish?
options: That cattle are a dead-end host with no onward transmission
A single spillover into cattle followed by cattle-to-cattle transmission
That bird and cattle viruses have been co-evolving in the same ecosystem
Repeated spillovers from a single geographically restricted bird population
quiz.explanation: Repeated independent spillovers would place cattle sequences scattered among bird sequences, each with its own recent bird ancestor. One clade means one successful jump — and it redirected the response from environmental biosecurity to cattle movement control.

quiz.question: Why could the H5N1 cattle finding not be expressed as 'H5N1 spilled into cattle'?
options: H5N1 refers to the whole genome whereas the finding concerned only the polymerase genes
Thousands of distinct viruses share that subtype, so it cannot identify one reassortant
H5N1 is a serological designation and cannot be assigned from sequence data
Subtype names are conventionally reserved for influenza viruses circulating in avian rather than mammalian hosts
quiz.explanation: H5N1 names two surface proteins; clade 2.3.4.4b names a haemagglutinin clade. The finding is about one specific combination of lineages across all eight segments, which only a genotype name — B3.13 — can carry.

quiz.question: A second, independent H5N1 genotype (D1.1) entered dairy cattle in January 2025. What does this show about the earlier single-spillover finding?
options: It was incorrect, and the cattle clade must have contained multiple introductions
It was an artefact of insufficient wild bird sequencing at the time
It applied only to the herds in the states affected during the first wave, and not to subsequent introductions
It was correct as a description of the past but did not bound future spillovers
quiz.explanation: Phylogenetic reconstruction describes what happened. Reading 'one spillover' as 'spillover is rare' is the error — and continued genomic surveillance is what caught the second event. A programme that stood down after the first finding would have missed it.

quiz.question: What bounds the confidence in the single-spillover conclusion?
options: The choice of discrete trait rather than structured coalescent phylogeography
The completeness of wild bird reservoir sequencing
The number of cattle sequences generated during the response
The absence of a molecular clock calibration for bovine-adapted lineages
quiz.explanation: Under-sampling the source population makes multiple similar introductions collapse into one apparent clade. Bird surveillance is far less dense than cattle response sequencing became, so the honest reading is one dominant introduction that established, plus any that did not establish or were not sampled.

exercises.label: Conceptual
exercises.prompt: The single-spillover finding was correct and a programme that stood down after it would have missed the second introduction. Explain the reasoning error in one sentence, then say what it implies about how surveillance findings should be worded.
exercises.guidance: Reading ‘one spillover happened’ as ‘spillover is rare’ confuses a reconstruction of the past with a bound on the future. Findings should be worded with their tense visible — ‘the cattle sequences descend from a single introduction in late 2023’ rather than ‘H5N1 entered cattle once’ — because the second phrasing quietly licenses a decision to stop looking.

exercises.label: Read the output
exercises.prompt: Segment-level lineage assignments for six influenza A isolates.
questions: All six are H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b. Why is that name useless for the epidemiological question here?
A-004 is from a cat and carries B3.13. What does that represent, and what does it change about the risk assessment?
A-005 and A-006 share a genotype and differ in host. What are the two readings, and what would distinguish them?
exercises.guidance: Every isolate here shares the subtype and the HA clade, so neither name distinguishes the two events — only the genotype, a combination across all eight segments, can. A-004 is spillback: a lineage exiting the cattle clade into another species, which means cattle have become a source rather than only a sink, and that is a change in the risk assessment rather than a detail. A-005 and A-006 could represent a fresh bird-to-cattle introduction (the D1.1 event of January 2025) or cattle-to-bird transmission; the tree topology distinguishes them — whether the cattle sequence is nested inside bird diversity or sits basal to it — and the confidence depends entirely on how densely the bird reservoir was sampled.

exercises.label: Three of six
exercises.prompt: Exactly three of these statements are correct.

statements.text: A single monophyletic clade of cattle sequences is consistent with one successful cross-species jump.
Genotype names are needed for influenza because segments reassort independently.
PB2 M631L being fixed across the cattle clade proves it increases mammalian transmissibility.
Dense sampling of the cattle population is what bounds confidence in the single-spillover conclusion.
The virus spread between states through movement of asymptomatic or presymptomatic animals.
Host-state reconstruction is a fundamentally different method from geographic phylogeography.

exercises.guidance: 1, 2 and 5. A fixed adaptation marker is a hypothesis about phenotype; the inference that it matters rests on experimental work in cells and animals, not on its presence in a tree. Statement 4 inverts the real limitation: it is sampling of the SOURCE population, the wild birds, that bounds the conclusion, because under-sampling there makes several similar introductions collapse into one apparent clade. Cattle were sequenced densely and that is not what constrains the inference. And host-state reconstruction is the same machinery as geographic phylogeography with host substituted for location.

exercises.label: Scaffolded
exercises.prompt: Apply the one-clade-versus-many logic to a reservoir question of your own. The frame is given.
exercises.output:
Pathogen: ______________   Suspected reservoir host: ______________

  If maintained in the reservoir, I expect the tree to show: ______________
  If repeated spillover from humans, I expect: ______________
  Sampling I would need before either conclusion is safe: ______________
  The bound I could honestly report with the sampling I actually have: ______________
exercises.guidance: Maintained: a monophyletic clade of reservoir-host sequences with its own internal diversity, and human sequences nested within or descending from it. Repeated spillback from humans: reservoir-host sequences scattered across human diversity, each with a recent human ancestor. The sampling you need is comparable intensity across hosts in the same foci over the same period — absolute numbers matter far less than the ratio. And the last line is the honest one: with human-dominated sampling, the report is a bound, not a point estimate.

lessons.title: Resistance as genomic surveillance — malaria and TB, or genomics without trees
lessons.subtitle: The most decision-linked genomics in global health, and the most deployable
lessons.description: Marker surveillance as a distinct discipline: kelch13 and pfhrp2/3 deletions, the WHO TB mutation catalogue built from 52,000 matched isolates, where tNGS sits in the diagnostic algorithm, and the five failure modes of marker surveillance.
lessons.practical: Take a resistance marker in your field. Is it validated or candidate? What decision and threshold does it feed? And what sampling frame would the frequency estimate need to justify that decision?

quiz.question: Why is malaria genomic surveillance mostly a marker discipline rather than a tree discipline?
options: Malaria transmission is too slow for phylogenetic resolution at outbreak scale
Plasmodium genomes are too large to align across many samples
Parasite DNA cannot be recovered at sufficient depth from routine blood samples
Sexual recombination in the mosquito means no single tree describes the genome
quiz.explanation: Recombination every transmission cycle shreds linkage, so different genomic regions have different histories. Combined with frequent multi-clone infections, consensus-based tree reasoning is compromised at the root — while the urgent questions are answerable from a handful of positions.

quiz.question: What makes the WHO TB mutation catalogue the model artefact for marker surveillance?
options: It is updated continuously, incorporating each new resistance mutation as it is reported anywhere in the literature
It replaces phenotypic drug susceptibility testing entirely for the drugs it covers
It covers every anti-TB medicine in current clinical use worldwide, including those still in trial phases
It is a genotype-phenotype association study at scale, with graded confidence per mutation
quiz.explanation: Built from over 52,000 isolates with matched whole genome sequencing and phenotypic testing, grading mutations for 13 medicines, it constructs the mutation-to-phenotype bridge explicitly and once, for everyone. It does not replace phenotypic testing, which remains needed for discordance and discovery.

quiz.question: Why does a 'susceptible' genotypic result not guarantee a susceptible organism?
options: Catalogues are updated too infrequently to include recent mutations
Resistance mechanisms not yet in the catalogue produce resistant organisms with susceptible genotypes
Genotypic testing has lower analytical sensitivity than culture-based methods
Consensus genomes average across the bacterial population and cannot detect resistance mutations at all
quiz.explanation: Efflux, unknown loci and epistatic combinations all produce phenotypic resistance invisible to a marker panel. Genotypic susceptibility prediction has sensitivity below 1, which is precisely why phenotypic testing is not obsolete.

quiz.question: A national survey reports 8% pfhrp2/3 double deletions among isolates from a referral hospital treating suspected treatment failures. What is the problem with using this to trigger a national RDT switch?
options: Reliable deletion calling requires whole genome rather than targeted sequencing, which this survey did not perform
Eight percent is below all published action thresholds for RDT replacement
Referral isolates are not a random sample, so the national prevalence is likely inflated
Double deletions must always be confirmed by protein-level testing before any programmatic action is taken
quiz.explanation: A frequency is a proportion and needs a representative sampling frame. Isolates enriched for treatment failure are enriched for exactly the phenotype under study, and using them for a national estimate can trigger an expensive and unnecessary procurement change.

quiz.question: What is the principal advantage of targeted NGS from sputum over whole genome sequencing from culture in TB?
options: It detects a broader set of resistance mechanisms including unknown loci
It requires no reference catalogue for interpretation of results
No culture wait, works on paucibacillary specimens, and detects minority resistant populations
It produces a complete closed genome that is also suitable for downstream transmission analysis
quiz.explanation: tNGS amplifies a defined panel directly from specimen and sequences it deeply. That removes the culture delay, works where bacillary load is low, and reaches heteroresistance that a consensus genome hides. It covers fewer loci than WGS, not more.

exercises.label: Conceptual
exercises.prompt: Why is a curated, graded genotype-phenotype catalogue described as more valuable than any individual study in a marker programme, and what does its absence cost a pathogen that lacks one?
exercises.guidance: Because it builds the mutation-to-phenotype bridge once, explicitly, with stated confidence, for everyone — converting a sequence into a susceptibility prediction with a known evidence level. Without one, resistance markers are scattered across the literature at varying evidence quality with no grading, so every programme rebuilds the interpretation layer privately and inconsistently. Building the catalogue is the rate-limiting step for extending marker surveillance to a new pathogen, and it is unglamorous, expensive and worth more than another sequencer.

exercises.prompt: A targeted NGS resistance report from sputum. Answer the three questions.
exercises.output:

---------------------------------------------------------------------

exercises.guidance: A consensus genome reports the majority base, so at 11% katG S315T would have been discarded entirely and the sample called katG-wild-type — while a resistant subpopulation is present and under treatment pressure will be selected. Heteroresistance is the clinical reason deep targeted sequencing exists. An uncertain-significance variant is not a resistance call: report it, flag it for phenotypic testing, and do not change the regimen on it alone — the graded confidence in the catalogue exists precisely to stop that. And absence of a known pncA variant means no catalogued resistance mechanism was detected; it does not mean the isolate is susceptible, because genotypic prediction has sensitivity below 1 and mechanisms outside the catalogue produce resistant organisms with 'susceptible' genotypes.

Referral isolates from suspected treatment failures are enriched for the phenotype under study, so using them nationally inflates the estimate and can trigger an unnecessary and expensive procurement change. And the validated/candidate distinction is the operational content of the marker list — only validated markers trigger policy.
